Foveated 2.5D semantic mapping from LiDAR

A complete architecture and build plan for a research prototype that turns raw LiDAR into a variable-resolution, semantically labelled elevation map, with an analysis of your MATLAB / Driving Scenario Designer export and a plan for using it.

Map
4 nested levels, 512² cells each
Cells
5 / 10 / 20 / 40 cm
Coverage
±12.8 to ±102.4 m
Memory
12 MiB core layers
Target
10 Hz, p99 ≤ 100 ms

Your frame_00008.pcd in bird's-eye view, with the first two levels of the recommended grid drawn on top. Everything on this page is designed around what this picture shows: the sensor sees its own car, cannot see the ground near the vehicle, and returns only a handful of points on distant, partly hidden objects.

·Summary of the recommendation

The recommended system is a single multi-task sparse-voxel network feeding a world-aligned, ego-centred, power-of-two nested Cartesian grid (a clipmap) whose cells store mergeable statistics, with objects kept as a separate, resolution-independent list and a decay-based temporal fusion layer. In one paragraph:

Points are cleaned, de-skewed and levelled; a sparse 3D U-Net (spconv 2.x, PyTorch) labels every point into a 10-class navigation taxonomy and, in later phases, predicts a coarse ground-height raster and centre-based object boxes. Labelled points are scattered into four nested 512 × 512 grids with 5 / 10 / 20 / 40 cm cells covering ±12.8 / ±25.6 / ±51.2 / ±102.4 m. Every level is quantised from one integer lattice, so a coarse cell is exactly the union of its four children: no gaps, overlaps or misalignment by construction. Cells keep additive statistics (counts, sums, min/max, class evidence), so coarse levels and temporal fusion are exact merges rather than resampling. Ground elevation is filled into unobserved cells with a pull–push pass over the pyramid; slope, step height, roughness, clearance and traversability are derived per level. Moving objects are tracked as boxes and kept out of the static map. The whole map is ~1.05 M cells (≈12 MB for the core layers), the same cell budget as a uniform 20 cm grid, and 16× fewer cells than a uniform 5 cm grid over the same area.

Decision Choice Main reason
Perception Sparse 3D U-Net + point branch, multi-task heads (semantics → ground height → centre-based boxes) Best accuracy/latency balance for outdoor LiDAR; PointNet++ is too slow and too weak at this scale
Moving vs static Per-point movable class + motion state from tracking (optional 2-sweep input) A single scan cannot tell a parked car from a moving one
Map structure 4-level clipmap, 512² per level, square rings, world-aligned lattice, toroidal scrolling Dense arrays (GPU/cache friendly), O(1) lookup, exact nesting, no resampling on motion
Resolution law Distance-based (cell ∝ range, factor 2 per level), plus velocity look-ahead offset as an option Matches how LiDAR sampling itself degrades with range; content-adaptive refinement cannot create information the sensor did not capture
Cell content Two-height 2.5D (ground, obstacle bottom, obstacle top) + class + confidence + traversability; extended layers optional Plain single-height 2.5D loses overhangs and mixes poles with ground
Aggregation Additive statistics; max/any for obstacles; summed class-probability evidence Exact across levels and over time; thin and distant obstacles are never averaged away
Temporal Pose-compensated accumulation with lazy exponential decay, visibility-based clearing, 3D Kalman tracker Fills the sparse near field; removes ghosts of moved objects
Software Python 3.10 + PyTorch for everything first; C++/CUDA + TensorRT only for deployment One language until profiling proves otherwise
Visualisation Rerun (development dashboard); Foxglove only if ROS 2 is adopted Timeline scrubbing, point clouds, images and metrics in one viewer
Data Your MATLAB simulation for controlled experiments and exact ground truth; SemanticKITTI as the main real benchmark; nuScenes for detection, tracking and a sparser sensor Each source covers a gap the others leave

0Section 0: What your MATLAB frame tells us

Before designing anything, I parsed frame_00008.pcd (ASCII PCD v0.7, 6.5 MB). The facts below drive several decisions later in this document.

Observation Measured value Consequence
Layout Organised 101 × 2251 = 227,351 points, stored column-major (MATLAB order) Read with order="F" or permute before export; the organised form is a ready-made range image
Beams 101 rows from +20° to −20° at 0.4°; 2251 columns at 0.16° over 360° Uniform beams (real sensors are not); set this to mimic your target sensor
Valid returns 52,878 (23 %); invalid rows are NaN with labels 0 Keep the NaN mask: it is free-space evidence later
Frame Sensor frame; road at z = −1.60 m (±0.02) Sensor is 1.60 m above the road; transform to a ground-level base frame
Self-hits 30,062 points (57 % of valid) are on the ego vehicle (actor 1, range 0.5–2.4 m) Must be removed before anything else; in real data this is an ego-box crop
Maximum range No return beyond 28.7 m; the next ground ring would land at ≈32.7 m Max range looks like ~30 m; set 100–120 m to exercise a 100 m design
Near-field blind zone No ground returns inside 4.4 m (= 1.60 / tan 20°) About 19 % of the 10 m fovea is never observed from a standstill
Ground sampling Ring spacing 0.11 m at 5 m, 0.44 m at 10 m, 1.75 m at 20 m A 5 cm grid is far finer than the ground sampling; see the fill-ratio chart
Fovea occupancy Only 5,442 of 125,663 5 cm cells within 10 m contain any point (4.3 %) Single-frame 5 cm maps are mostly empty; accumulation or inpainting is required
Labels class_id 1 car, 2 truck, 3 bicycle, 4 pedestrian, 6 guardrail/barrier segments (actors 10001–10005, 20001–20004), 7 road Free, exact per-point and per-instance ground truth
Distant object Bicycle: 4 points at 27 m, shadowed by a truck A realistic test of distant and occluded object handling
ID precision Road actor_id stored as float32 = 4294983680 (above 2²⁴, so not exactly representable) Write IDs as unsigned integers, never float
material_id All NaN Fix or drop the field
Intensity Per-class means differ strongly (road ≈ 51, car ≈ 103, pedestrian ≈ 210, truck ≈ 250) Synthetic intensity is almost a label; a network trained on it will cheat. Drop or randomise it for sim-to-real
Scene content Flat road mesh only; no off-road ground, curbs, potholes, poles or buildings Driving Scenario Designer alone cannot train or test terrain analysis; add RoadRunner scenes (§21)

The same frame as an organised range image (rows above +8° are empty and cropped). Colours match the bird's-eye view: dark grey is the ego vehicle, light grey the road. The dark band at the bottom is the sensor looking at its own car.

How far apart LiDAR samples are at each range for your sensor settings, compared with the proposed cell sizes. Cell size tracks the horizontal and vertical sample spacing on upright objects closely at every level. Ground rings spread out quadratically, so no fixed grid can be "filled" by one scan beyond a few metres.

Measured on your frame: share of each distance band whose cells contain at least one road point, for four cell sizes. Part of each annulus is off-road (and therefore empty in this scene), so compare the bars with each other rather than reading them as absolute coverage.

The lesson is the most important hidden problem in the brief: the 5 cm "fovea" is finer than what the sensor delivers. The high-resolution region only pays off if the design (a) accumulates scans over time using ego motion, (b) fills ground surfaces from coarser levels, and (c) never pretends that an empty cell is free space.

1Section 1: Requirements analysis

Requirements marked E are explicit in the brief; I are implicit but necessary for the system to work.

1.1 Functional requirements

ID Requirement Src
F1 Ingest raw LiDAR scans (organised or unorganised) with timestamps E/I
F2 Classify every point into terrain / static obstacle / dynamic object classes E
F3 Separate drivable from non-drivable surface E
F4 Estimate ground elevation and terrain features (slope, steps/curbs, roughness, depressions) E
F5 Detect and classify static obstacles (walls, poles, barriers) and dynamic objects (pedestrians, vehicles, cyclists) E
F6 Project classified points into a variable-resolution 2.5D grid with semantic layers E
F7 Cell size grows with distance (fine near, coarse far) E
F8 No alignment errors, gaps, overlaps or discontinuities between resolution regions E
F9 Visualise the map with class colours and show memory savings E
F10 Report latency, FPS and distance-binned accuracy E
F11 Remove self-returns, invalid returns and out-of-range points I
F12 Transform points into a gravity-aligned frame (otherwise elevations are wrong) I
F13 Represent unknown / unobserved space explicitly, distinct from free space I
F14 Represent overhanging structures (clearance) I (brief mentions overhangs)
F15 Distinguish moving from movable objects I
F16 Compensate ego motion when combining scans I

1.2 Non-functional, performance and real-time requirements

ID Requirement Assumed target
N1 Real-time at sensor rate 10 Hz input; end-to-end latency p95 ≤ 100 ms, target mean ≤ 60 ms on a workstation GPU
N2 Bounded, predictable memory Fixed-size map independent of drive length; ≤ 64 MB for the extended map
N3 Deterministic, testable geometry Bit-identical grid results for identical inputs
N4 Modular: grids, models and datasets swappable by configuration Needed for fair baselines
N5 Deployable on an edge device with stated compromises Jetson AGX Orin class, ≥ 10 Hz with reduced settings
N6 Reproducible experiments Seeds, pinned environments, versioned data and configs

1.3 Perception, mapping, visualisation and evaluation requirements

  • Perception: per-point semantics over a fixed taxonomy; object instances with class, position, extent, heading and velocity for movable classes; accuracy reported per distance band.
  • Mapping: fine cells within at least 10 m, coarse cells to at least 100 m; per-cell elevation, obstacle heights, class, confidence, traversability; temporal consistency; stale-data removal.
  • Visualisation: raw and labelled points, per-layer map views, cell boundaries per level, objects and tracks, live performance metrics, side-by-side uniform vs foveated.
  • Evaluation: perception metrics, representation fidelity, efficiency, system-level latency; baselines and ablations; accuracy–cost trade-off curves.

1.4 Ambiguities, contradictions and assumptions

# Issue in the brief Why it matters Assumption / resolution
A1 "5 cm within 10 m, 50 cm up to 100 m": 50/5 = 10 is not a power of two Nested cells only align exactly with power-of-two ratios Use 5 → 10 → 20 → 40 cm (or 6.25 → 50 cm if 50 cm is mandatory); both are configurable
A2 "Radius" implies circular regions Square cells cannot tile a circle boundary without partial cells Square (Chebyshev) rings; the 10 m disc sits inside the ±12.8 m fine square
A3 5 cm cells at 10 m are finer than LiDAR ground sampling Mostly empty fovea per scan (4.3 % in your frame) Temporal accumulation + pull–push ground filling + explicit unknown state
A4 "Segment into … moving objects" from a network A single scan has no motion information Network predicts movable; motion comes from tracking or multi-sweep input
A5 "Memory reduction compared to a uniform high-resolution 3D map" Almost any 2.5D map beats a dense 3D grid; this is a straw man Compare against uniform 2.5D grids and a sparse 3D map as well
A6 "Without … data loss" Every aggregation loses information Define measurable loss of navigation-relevant information (§26)
A7 "High FPS" Useful FPS is capped by the sensor (10–20 Hz) Report latency percentiles and headroom rather than raw FPS
A8 "2.5D grid" Single height per cell cannot represent bridges, branches, barrier arms Store ground height plus obstacle bottom and top
A9 "High accuracy … across varying distances" No metric defined Distance-binned mIoU, AP and recall (§26)
A10 Map frame not specified Ego-rotating grids must be resampled every frame (aliasing) Gravity-aligned, yaw-fixed (odometry) frame, translated with the vehicle
A11 Drivable vs non-drivable "Drivable" is a rule (a sidewalk is flat but not drivable); "traversable" is physics Keep separate semantic and geometric layers
A12 Potholes Negative obstacles are mostly occluded and only visible at short range Near-field detection only; unobserved on-road holes flagged as unknown
A13 PointNet++ named as an example Too slow and too weak for full outdoor scans (§7) Sparse convolution backbone
A14 Sensor model not stated Resolution design depends on beam geometry Assume 32–128 beams, 0.1–0.4° resolution, 100–120 m range, 10 Hz; your sim uses 101 beams at 0.4°, 0.16°
A15 Which "distance": sensor, vehicle centre, or path? Level placement Distance from the vehicle reference point projected on the ground plane

2Section 2: System design questions

These are the decisions that shape everything else; each is answered in the section noted.

  1. Perception input: raw points, voxels, range image, BEV pillars or polar cells? (§3.1, §7)
  2. One model or several? Semantics, detection and ground height as shared-backbone heads or separate networks? (§7)
  3. Where does "moving" come from? Network, multi-sweep input, or tracking? (§9, §10)
  4. What exactly is 2.5D here? One height, height statistics, or a small stack of heights? (§14)
  5. Resolution law: distance only, or also semantics, risk, uncertainty, velocity? (§11)
  6. Data structure: nested grids, quadtree, polar grid, hash map? (§12)
  7. Map frame: sensor-fixed, vehicle-fixed, or world-aligned and translating? (§11, §13)
  8. Cross-level consistency: how to guarantee that coarse cells agree with fine cells? (§13)
  9. Aggregation: which statistic for which layer, and are they mergeable over levels and time? (§15)
  10. Ground under objects and between rings: leave empty, interpolate, or learn? (§8)
  11. Temporal fusion: accumulate at all? how to forget, how to remove moved objects? (§10)
  12. Dynamic objects in a 2.5D map: rasterise, keep as a list, or both? (§9, §16)
  13. Distant sparse objects: can resolution adaptation help, or is something else needed? (§16)
  14. Real-time execution: what runs on GPU vs CPU, sync vs async? (§18)
  15. Language and deployment: Python only, C++ core, or Rust? TensorRT path for sparse convolutions? (§19, §36)
  16. Evaluation: how to compare representations fairly when their cells differ? (§26, §27)

3Section 3: Alternative approaches and decisions

3.1 How the network sees the point cloud

Option Examples Accuracy (outdoor semantics) Latency Memory Deployment Verdict
Point-based, set abstraction PointNet++ Low on full outdoor scans (≈20 mIoU reported on SemanticKITTI) Slow: farthest-point sampling and ball queries on 10⁵ points Moderate Custom ops Reject
Point-based, efficient RandLA-Net Medium Medium Low Custom ops (kNN) Not preferred
Point transformer (serialised) Point Transformer V3 Highest reported Medium; attention kernels High Hard (TensorRT) Upper-bound research baseline only
Range image 2D CNN RangeNet++, SalsaNext, FIDNet, CENet Medium–good Fastest Low Easy (pure 2D, TensorRT) Edge fallback; natural fit for your organised export
Sparse 3D voxel CNN MinkUNet, SPVCNN, Cylinder3D Good–very good Fast with spconv/TorchSparse Scales with occupied voxels Moderate (NVIDIA libspconv) Primary
BEV pillars 2D CNN PointPillars-style, PolarNet Medium; weak on vertical detail Fast Grid-sized Easy Good for detection heads, not for per-point semantics
Classical geometry only Ground fit + clustering No semantics Fast Low Easy Baseline only

Range-image networks blur object boundaries when labels are projected back to points (a kNN clean-up is needed) and depend on the sensor's exact scan pattern. Sparse voxel networks are sensor-agnostic, which matters because you will train on real data from one sensor and test on simulated data from another.

3.2 Map data structure

Option Lookup Insert Neighbours GPU Consistency across resolutions Verdict
Uniform dense grid O(1) O(1) Trivial Excellent n/a (single resolution) Baseline
Two-region grid (brief's example) O(1) O(1) Seam at one boundary Good Only if ratio is 2ᵏ Baseline
Clipmap (nested dense grids) O(1) O(L) per point Trivial within level; parent/child by bit shift Excellent Exact by construction Selected
Quadtree (pointer) O(depth) O(depth) Awkward Poor Good Reject for online use
Linear quadtree (Morton keys, sorted/hashed) O(1)–O(log n) O(1) amortised Moderate Moderate Good Only for content-adaptive research extension
Polar / log-polar grid O(1) O(1) Anisotropic Good Rings align; translation needs resampling Baseline; poor for accumulation
Spatial hash of fine cells O(1) expected O(1) Moderate Moderate Good Used for optional refinement tiles
3D voxel / octree (OctoMap) O(depth) O(depth) Good Poor Good Baseline for the "3D map" comparison

3.3 Resolution law

Option Justification Cost Risk Verdict
Distance only Sensor sampling degrades with range; safety relevance falls with distance Zero runtime cost, fixed memory Misses near-path importance at speed Essential
Distance + velocity look-ahead (shift the fine region forward) Stopping distance grows with speed Negligible Less coverage behind the car Recommended option
Semantic / risk refinement (finer tiles around objects) Planning precision around hazards Variable memory, complexity Refining beyond sampling density adds no information Research extension
Uncertainty / terrain-complexity driven Spend cells where the surface is rough Variable Unstable cell layout over time Research extension
Density-adaptive (quadtree splits on point count) Cells follow data Variable Layout changes every frame; hard to fuse over time Baseline only

3.4 Other decisions (short form)

Question Options considered Decision
Ground estimation RANSAC plane, line-fit, Patchwork++, CSF, learned height, hybrid Hybrid: learned ground classes + robust per-cell statistics + pull–push filling + learned coarse height for occluded ground
Instances Clustering, panoptic head, centre-based detection Clustering in the MVP; centre-based boxes (CenterPoint-style head) in the final system
Motion Multi-scan network, scene flow, tracking Tracking (required anyway); 2-sweep input as an ablation
Temporal map None, occupancy log-odds, decayed statistics, full SLAM Decayed statistics with known poses; odometry from ground truth (sim/datasets) or KISS-ICP on real data
Free-space clearing 2D ray casting per point, range-image visibility test Range-image visibility test (cost scales with obstacle cells, not rays)
Core language Python, C++, Rust Python + PyTorch first; C++/CUDA for deployment kernels; Rust rejected (no sparse-conv/TensorRT ecosystem)
Middleware ROS 2, none None in the core; thin ROS 2 adapter later

4.1 Online components

Tightly coupled: voxeliser ↔ network (same voxel size and coordinate convention), grid engine ↔ terrain derivation (share layer tensors). Independent: dataset readers, tracker, visualiser, evaluation, ROS adapter.

5Section 5: Sensor and data pipeline

5.1 Point attributes

Attribute Type Needed for Required?
x, y, z float32 Everything Yes
Intensity / reflectivity float32 or uint8 Lane markings, road vs terrain; drop for sim-to-real Optional feature
Row (beam) and column uint16 Range image, visibility test, deskew Yes if available
Per-point time offset float32 (s) Deskew on real spinning sensors Yes on real data; zero in your sim
Return index uint8 Rain/vegetation handling Optional
Labels (class, instance) uint32 packed Training and evaluation Offline only

5.2 Coordinate frames

Frame Definition Notes
S (sensor) LiDAR origin, x forward, y left, z up Your PCD is in S
B (base) Vehicle reference point on the ground, same axes ISO 8855 / ROS REP-103 convention; Driving Scenario Designer uses the rear-axle centre on the ground
M (map) Gravity-aligned z, yaw fixed to odometry, origin at a world lattice point The grid lives here
W (world) Global odometry / scenario frame float64 poses

p_M = T_MW · T_WB(t) · T_BS · p_S. Compose poses in float64; convert to float32 only for points relative to the map anchor (float32 has ~1 mm resolution at 10 km, which is too coarse for 5 cm cells after long drives if you use absolute coordinates).

Levelling matters. A 1° pitch error produces r·tan(1°) = 0.17 m of elevation error at 10 m and 1.75 m at 100 m. Roll and pitch must come from an IMU or the pose; in simulation they come from the scenario.

5.3 Processing order

1  decode             → xyz, intensity, row, col, t_offset, valid mask (NaN / zero range)
2  range gate         → drop r < r_min (0.3 m) and r > r_max (config, 120 m)
3  ego filter         → drop points inside vehicle box + 0.2 m margin (sim: also actor_id == ego)
4  deskew             → p_i ← T_WB(t0)⁻¹ · T_WB(t0 + t_i) · p_i   (skip when t_i = 0)
5  to base frame      → apply T_BS
6  crop               → |x|,|y| ≤ 102.4 m;  z within [−5, +6] m of base
7  voxelise (GPU)     → sparse tensor for the network (keeps point→voxel index)
8  infer              → per-point class probabilities (+ BEV heads)
9  to map frame       → apply T_MB (levelling + translation)
10 grid insert        → statistics per level

5.4 Where information may be removed, and where it must not

Safe to remove Harmful to remove
NaN / zero-range returns (but keep the mask for free space) Isolated points at long range (may be the only evidence of a pedestrian)
Self-hits and returns inside the vehicle box Low-intensity points (dark cars, wet asphalt)
Points above the clearance ceiling (e.g. > 6 m above ground) Points near curbs before ground estimation (averaging erases the step)
Points beyond the map extent Near-field points before perception (random or voxel downsampling hurts small objects)
Exact duplicates Points of the "noise/outlier" class before evaluation (report separately)

Avoid statistical outlier removal (kNN per point) online: it is slow and deletes sparse distant objects. Use the network's outlier class and temporal persistence instead.

5.5 Timing, synchronisation and batching

  • Every scan carries stamp_ns (monotonic, start of sweep) and, on real sensors, per-point offsets derived from the column index: t_i = col_i / W · T_sweep for a spinning LiDAR.
  • Poses are interpolated at stamp_ns (and per point for deskew) with linear translation + SLERP rotation.
  • Hardware sync on a vehicle: PTP (IEEE 1588) for LiDAR, IMU and compute.
  • Online batch size is 1 (latency). Training uses batches of 4–8 scans packed as one sparse tensor with a batch-index column.
  • Your simulation is instantaneous per frame, so deskew is a no-op; keep the code path, because real data needs it.

6Section 6: Data representation at each stage

Stage Representation Why
Sensor output Organised range image H × W (rows = beams) Native; free neighbourhoods; carries the "no return" mask
Preprocessing Flat point arrays + row/col indices Cheap filtering and transforms
Network input Sparse voxel tensor (10 cm), plus point features Sensor-agnostic, memory scales with occupied space
Network internals Sparse 3D at strides 1–8; dense BEV at 40 cm for heads 3D for semantics, 2D for boxes and ground height
Network output Per-point probabilities (FP16, K = 10), BEV rasters, box list Points keep full geometric precision until the map
Map Clipmap: L dense 2D tensors (per layer) with toroidal offsets O(1) access, GPU-friendly, fixed memory
Objects List of boxes and tracks (float32) Resolution-independent; no rasterisation loss
Transmission Hollow rings (fine region only once) + sparse/delta encoding + zstd No duplicate data
Visualisation Decimated points, per-level images / meshes, line strips for cell borders Keeps the viewer responsive
Evaluation Common 5 cm reference lattice and point-level queries Fair comparison between different grids

7Section 7: Deep-learning architecture

7.1 Project taxonomy

A small navigation-oriented taxonomy keeps training data from different sources compatible and makes the map layers meaningful.

ID Class Group SemanticKITTI source classes nuScenes-lidarseg Your MATLAB export
0 ignore — unlabeled, outlier noise, ignore invalid, ego (actor 1)
1 drivable terrain road, parking, lane-marking driveable_surface 7 road
2 sidewalk terrain sidewalk sidewalk — (add in RoadRunner)
3 terrain terrain terrain, other-ground terrain, other_flat —
4 structure static building, fence, other-structure manmade, barrier 5 jersey barrier, 6 guardrail
5 pole-like static pole, traffic-sign, trunk (part of manmade) —
6 vegetation static vegetation vegetation —
7 vehicle movable car, truck, bus, other-vehicle (+ moving variants) car, truck, bus, trailer, construction 1 car, 2 truck
8 two-wheeler movable bicycle, motorcycle, bicyclist, motorcyclist bicycle, motorcycle 3 bicycle
9 pedestrian movable person pedestrian 4 pedestrian
10 other obstacle static other-object traffic_cone, debris, pushable —

"Moving" is a separate binary attribute (SemanticKITTI provides moving labels; nuScenes provides box velocities; your simulation provides actor velocities). Check the class IDs in your scenario's class specification; the table uses Driving Scenario Designer defaults and what your frame shows.

7.2 Network

The network runs in a gravity-aligned, yaw-fixed frame whose voxel lattice is the map lattice: points are levelled and rotated into the map frame M (translation relative to the snapped map centre) before voxelisation. Then 10 cm voxels coincide with level-1 cells, stride 2 with level 2 and stride 4 with level 3, so network rasters drop into the map without any resampling. The cost is that the network must be rotation-invariant, which standard random-yaw augmentation already provides; the vehicle heading can be given back as an extra point feature if an ablation shows it helps.

input      N points, features f = [x, y, z, range, (intensity), (Δt)]        N ≈ 20k–260k
voxelise   10 cm dynamic voxelisation (no point cap), PFN: Linear-BN-ReLU → scatter-mean
encoder    s1: SubMConv3d 32  ×2 ResBlocks
           s2: SparseConv3d ↓ → 64   ×2
           s4: ↓ → 128 ×2
           s8: ↓ → 256 ×2
           s16: ↓ → 256 ×2
decoder    inverse convs back to s1 with skip concatenation (U-Net)
points     point MLP branch, fused with devoxelised features at s1 and s4 (SPVCNN-style)
heads      H1 semantics      per point: Linear → K = 10 logits (class 0 is ignored in the loss)
           H2 ground height  s4 features collapsed over z → dense 512×512 (40 cm) →
                             3×Conv2d → [height, log σ, valid logit]
           H3 objects        same BEV → CenterPoint-style: heatmap(3 movable classes),
                             centre offset, z, log(l,w,h), sin/cos yaw, (velocity)
           H4 motion (opt.)  per point: moving logit (needs ≥ 2 sweeps as input)
Choice Default Alternatives for ablation
Voxel size 10 cm 5 cm (more accurate, slower), 20 cm; cylindrical partition (distance-adaptive)
Width 32-64-128-256-256 ×0.5 for edge, ×1.5 for accuracy
Library spconv 2.x TorchSparse++ (faster kernels, harder install)
Upper-bound backbone — Point Transformer V3 via Pointcept
Edge backbone — Range-image CNN (FIDNet/CENet-style) + kNN refinement

7.3 One model or several?

One shared backbone with heads. Semantics, ground height and boxes all need the same geometric features; a second network would roughly double the dominant cost of the pipeline. The risk is negative transfer between tasks, so training is staged (§22): semantics alone first, then add the ground and object heads and fine-tune jointly. The single-task model stays as a baseline, which makes "is multi-task worth it?" an explicit ablation.

7.4 Output representation

  • Per-point class probabilities (FP16, top-k = 3 retained to save memory) and argmax.
  • Ground-height raster (40 cm, map frame) with log-variance and validity.
  • Boxes: (x, y, z, l, w, h, yaw, vx, vy, class, score) in the map frame.
  • Optional per-point moving probability.

8Section 8: Terrain perception

8.1 Why hybrid

Method Strength Weakness
Geometric (Patchwork++, line fit, RANSAC) No training, predictable, fast Confuses low vegetation, ramps and sidewalks; no semantics
Learned semantics Knows road vs sidewalk vs grass, handles clutter Can be confidently wrong out of distribution; gives labels, not heights
Learned height regression Estimates ground under cars and in gaps Blurry; needs dense height ground truth
Hybrid Semantics decide which points are ground, geometry measures where the ground is, learning fills what was not seen More components to test

Drivable is a semantic decision (a sidewalk is flat but not drivable). Traversable is a geometric decision (a road with a 20 cm step is not traversable). The map keeps both.

8.2 Ground surface per cell

Ground-class points (drivable, sidewalk, terrain) update, for every level ℓ containing them:

w_g ← w_g + 1          S_g ← S_g + z          Q_g ← Q_g + z²          zmin_g ← min(zmin_g, z)
ĥ   = S_g / w_g        σ²  = Q_g / w_g − ĥ²

Outlier gate: a ground-labelled point more than 0.3 m from its parent-level estimate is counted as non-ground and flagged (catches semantic errors on low objects).

8.3 Filling gaps: pull–push over the pyramid

Because every point is inserted into all levels that contain it (§13), coarse levels already hold the "pull" aggregates. The "push" step fills fine cells that have no ground evidence:

for ℓ = L−1 down to 0:
    for each cell c at level ℓ with w_g(c) < w_min:
        ĥ_p  = bilinear interpolation of level-(ℓ+1) heights at centre(c)
        σ²_c = σ²_p + (|∇h_p| · s_ℓ)² + σ²_interp
        ĥ_c  = (w_g(c)·ĥ_obs(c) + λ·ĥ_p) / (w_g(c) + λ)         λ = 1 by default
        flag(c) |= INPAINTED
at level L−1: fill remaining holes by normalised convolution
        ĥ = (G ∗ (w·h)) / (G ∗ w),   then fuse the network's height raster
        by inverse-variance weighting:  ĥ = (ĥ_obs/σ²_obs + ĥ_net/σ²_net) / (1/σ²_obs + 1/σ²_net)

Inpainted cells carry larger variance and a flag, so planners and metrics can treat them differently. This is what makes the 5 cm level usable despite 4 % single-scan occupancy.

8.4 Terrain features (computed on each level)

Feature Formula Use
Slope ∂h/∂x ≈ (h[i+1,j] − h[i−1,j]) / (2 s_ℓ), same for y; θ = atan(‖∇h‖) Ramps, banking
Step height Δ = max over 4-neighbours abs(h_c − h_n), observed cells only Curbs, kerbs, ledges
Roughness ρ = sqrt(σ²_within + residual² of a 3×3 plane fit) Gravel, rubble
Depression d = h − (G_σ ∗ h), candidate if d < −0.04 m over ≥ 4 cells on drivable ground Potholes (near field only)
Clearance c = zmin_obs − ĥ Overhangs, barrier arms, branches
Obstacle height o = zmax_obs − ĥ Obstacle severity

Curb logic: a step of 0.05–0.35 m on an edge whose two sides have different terrain classes (drivable ↔ sidewalk/terrain). Curbs can only be localised to ±s_ℓ/2, so they are reliable on levels 0–1 (≤ 25.6 m) and appear as "steep and rough" on coarser levels.

Negative obstacles: a pothole's floor is usually hidden at grazing angles. An unobserved patch of drivable surface surrounded by observed drivable cells, inside braking distance, is marked suspicious unknown instead of being inpainted.

8.5 Traversability

cost = 255                                 if cell is neither observed nor inpainted       (unknown)
cost = 254                                 if obstacle class and o > 0.15 m and c < H_vehicle + 0.2 m
                                           or Δ > step_max (0.15 m)  or θ > slope_max (15°)
cost = policy(class)                       for sidewalk / terrain (e.g. 200 or 254)
cost = min(253, 253 · Σ w_k · q_k)         otherwise, with q = [θ/θ_max, ρ/ρ_max, Δ/Δ_max,
                                                                1 − confidence, inpainted]

All thresholds are vehicle parameters in the configuration, not constants in code.

9Section 9: Object perception

Capability Needed? Reason
Per-point semantic segmentation Essential Feeds every map layer; handles static structures without instances
Object instances for movable classes Essential Needed for velocity, motion state and not smearing objects into the map
Geometric clustering of movable points Essential in MVP Cheap instances without box labels
Centre-based 3D detection head Recommended (final system) Amodal boxes for partial and distant objects, heading, velocity
Tracking Recommended Motion state, velocity, identity, temporal smoothing
Panoptic (per-point instance IDs for all classes) Unnecessary Individual wall or pole identities do not help navigation
Instances of static objects Unnecessary Semantic cells already describe them

9.1 MVP instances: clustering

Movable-class points are clustered in bird's-eye view with a range-dependent radius ε(r) = clamp(0.3 + 0.01·r, 0.3, 1.5) m (connected components on level-1 occupancy, or DBSCAN). An L-shape or minimum-area rectangle fit gives a box; height comes from the points.

9.2 Final instances: centre-based head

A CenterPoint-style head on the 40 cm BEV features predicts class heatmaps and box parameters, producing amodal boxes even when only one face of an object is visible. Its peaks also split adjacent objects (a pedestrian standing next to a car) better than clustering does.

9.3 Hard cases

Case Handling
Partially observed Amodal regression; track keeps a size prior per class
Distant and sparse Detection operates on points, not on the map; low-point detections kept with lower score; distance-binned thresholds (§16)
Overlapping in BEV (under a bridge, person next to a car) Per-point semantics keep classes apart; clearance layer keeps the bridge from hiding the car
Occluded Track coasting for up to 0.3 s; occluded cells stay unknown
Static unknown objects (debris) "Other obstacle" class plus geometric fallback: any non-ground point taller than 0.15 m above the ground surface is an obstacle regardless of class

The geometric fallback is a deliberate safety net: a semantic error must never delete an obstacle from the map.

10Section 10: Temporal processing

Temporal processing is necessary, not optional: the near field is otherwise mostly empty (§0), and "moving" cannot be known from one scan.

10.1 Components

Component Method Phase
Ego motion Scenario ground truth (sim), dataset poses (SemanticKITTI, nuScenes), KISS-ICP on real data P7
Deskew Per-point pose interpolation P7 (real data)
Accumulation Decayed additive statistics per cell P7
Stale data Lazy exponential decay with class-specific time constants P7
Moved objects Range-image visibility test (clearing) P7
Moving objects Tracker; tracked moving points bypass the static map P7–P8
Map motion Snapped recentring with hysteresis, toroidal scrolling P2

A local, decaying map tolerates odometry drift well: errors only matter over the few seconds a cell remembers.

10.2 Lazy decay

Each cell stores t_last. When a cell is touched at time t, its statistics are first multiplied by

f = exp(−(t − t_last) / τ_c)
w ← f·w + Σ w_i     S ← f·S + Σ w_i z_i     Q ← f·Q + Σ w_i z_i²     E_k ← f·E_k + Σ p_k(i)
t_last ← t

Readers apply the same factor on the fly, so untouched cells never need a per-frame pass. min/max statistics cannot be decayed exactly; they are reset to the new values whenever f < 0.5.

Class group τ_c Reason
Ground (drivable, sidewalk, terrain) 60 s Terrain does not change
Static (structure, pole, vegetation, other) 20 s Mostly permanent; allows slow correction
Movable but stationary (parked cars, standing people) 2 s May leave at any time
Moving (tracked, speed > 0.5 m/s) 0 (not accumulated) Kept in the per-frame dynamic layer and the object list

A cell whose effective weight falls below ε returns to unknown.

10.3 Class evidence

Class evidence is a decayed sum of per-point probabilities, E_k, which behaves like Dirichlet counts: class = argmax E_k, confidence = max E_k / Σ E_k. Summing log-probabilities instead would become overconfident after a few hundred points.

10.4 Visibility-based clearing

For every cell with obstacle evidence inside the current field of view:

project the cell centre (at mid obstacle height) into the current range image → (row, col), expected range r_e
r_m = measured range at (row, col) and its 3×3 neighbourhood
if all r_m > r_e + δ(r_e):   w_obs ← 0.3 · w_obs        # the beam passed through: object is gone
if any |r_m − r_e| ≤ δ:      confirm (no change)
if all r_m are NaN:          w_obs ← 0.8 · w_obs        # weak evidence (absorption or sky)
δ(r) = max(0.3 m, 2 · s_ℓ)

Cost scales with the number of obstacle cells (typically 10⁴–10⁵), not with rays × cells, and it needs the organised range image, which both real spinning sensors and your simulation provide.

10.5 Tracker

State [x, y, z, yaw, l, w, h, vx, vy], constant-velocity Kalman filter, greedy association on velocity-compensated centre distance with class-specific gates (pedestrian 1 m, two-wheeler 2 m, vehicle 4 m), birth after 2 hits, deletion after 3 misses at 10 Hz, motion state moving when speed > 0.5 m/s for 3 consecutive frames (hysteresis back to stationary below 0.3 m/s).

11Section 11: Variable-resolution (foveated) representation

11.1 What the sensor allows

For a spinning LiDAR with azimuth step Δφ, beam spacing Δθ and mount height h, the spacing between samples at horizontal range r is approximately

on upright surfaces, horizontally:   Δ_h(r) = r · Δφ
on upright surfaces, vertically:     Δ_v(r) = r · Δθ
on flat ground, radially:            Δ_g(r) ≈ r² · Δθ / h

With your settings (Δφ = 0.16°, Δθ = 0.4°, h = 1.6 m): Δ_h(10 m) = 2.8 cm, Δ_v(10 m) = 7 cm, Δ_g(10 m) = 44 cm; at 100 m: 28 cm, 70 cm and 44 m. One scan cannot support a cell smaller than the local sample spacing, and the spacing on objects grows linearly with range. The natural resolution law is therefore constant angular resolution:

s*(r) = κ · r,     clamped to [s_min, s_max],     Δφ ≲ κ ≲ Δθ

This is a log-polar law. It justifies distance-based foveation physically, not only as a heuristic.

11.2 Clipmap approximation of the law

Levels ℓ = 0 … L−1, each an n × n square grid centred on the vehicle:

s_ℓ = s₀ · 2^ℓ              cell size
E_ℓ = n · s_ℓ / 2           half-extent (Chebyshev radius)
α_ℓ(d) = s_ℓ / d ∈ [2/n, 4/n]   angular size of a cell in the ring E_{ℓ−1} ≤ d < E_ℓ
                            (d = Chebyshev distance; square corners reach √2 further)

So a clipmap is a Cartesian, power-of-two, piecewise-constant approximation of s = κ·r with κ between 2/n and 4/n. For n = 512 that is 0.22°–0.45°, which brackets your sensor's 0.16° × 0.4° sampling (the proposed-cell-size staircase in the spacing chart above).

Choosing the parameters

n  ≈ 2 / sqrt(Δφ · Δθ)                → 453 for 0.16° × 0.4°  → round to 512 (must be a multiple of 4)
s₀ = required near-field precision       → 5 cm (brief)
E₀ = n·s₀/2 ≥ R_fovea                    → 12.8 m ≥ 10 m ✓
L  = 1 + ceil(log2(R_max / E₀))          → R_max = 100 m → L = 4, E₃ = 102.4 m ✓
Level Cell Extent Cells Angular size in its ring
0 5 cm ±12.8 m 512² ≥ 0.22° (fine everywhere near)
1 10 cm ±25.6 m 512² (¾ owned) 0.22–0.45°
2 20 cm ±51.2 m 512² (¾ owned) 0.22–0.45°
3 40 cm ±102.4 m 512² (¾ owned) 0.22–0.45°

If exactly 50 cm at long range is required, use s₀ = 6.25 cm (6.25 / 12.5 / 25 / 50 cm, E₃ = 128 m with n = 512, or n = 400 for E₃ = 100 m). Never use 5 cm → 50 cm directly: the ratio is not a power of two, so cell edges cannot line up.

11.3 Is distance alone enough?

For the static and terrain map, yes: resolution beyond the sampling density adds cells but not information, and the sampling density is set by distance. The other candidates are better handled differently:

Driver Better mechanism than changing the grid
Semantic importance (a pedestrian at 60 m) Keep the object as a full-precision box in the object list; aggregate obstacles with max so a few points still mark the cell
Motion Tracker state, not grid cells
Uncertainty Variance layer; the layout stays fixed
Obstacle probability, risk Update and publish priority; optional refinement tiles (research)
Speed Velocity look-ahead: move the grid centre forward (below)

Velocity look-ahead (recommended option)

c = snap( p_ego + clamp(τ_la · v, 0, D_max) ,  s_{L−1} )        τ_la = 0.5 s

Constraint that keeps the required fine radius R_f behind the vehicle, given recentring hysteresis δ (§13.3):

D_max + δ ≤ E₀ − R_f          with E₀ = 12.8 m, R_f = 10 m  →  D_max + δ ≤ 2.8 m
e.g. δ = 1.6 m, D_max = 1.2 m;   or accept a smaller rear fovea when driving fast

Risk-driven refinement tiles (research extension). A sparse hash map of 32 × 32 patches at half the local cell size, activated for the top-K cells by

R(x) = P_obstacle(x) · exp(−d_path(x)² / 2σ²) / max(TTC(x), t_min)

It is only worth testing where the sampling supports it (azimuthally, a 20 cm cell at 30 m still has 8 cm spacing available). Expect a gain in planning precision around hazards, not in detection accuracy, because detection runs on points.

12Section 12: Grid data structure

12.1 Layout

Clipmap
  spec        : s₀, L, n, layer schema, decay constants
  center      : int64[2]   centre in units of the coarsest cell (world lattice)
  offset      : int32[L,2] toroidal storage offset per level
  t_now       : float64
  layers      : dict[name → Tensor[L, n, n, (C)]]     # struct of arrays, all levels stacked

Because every level has the same n, each layer is one tensor of shape [L, n, n]. A single convolution, pooling or scatter call processes all levels at once, which is the main practical advantage of an equal-n clipmap over a quadtree.

12.2 Operations

Operation Complexity Implementation
Point → cell (all levels) O(L) per point integer shift, bounds test
Cell lookup O(1) (u + offset) mod n
Insert N points O(N·L) index_add_, scatter_reduce_ (amin/amax)
Neighbourhood (3×3) O(1) per cell conv2d / unfold over [L, n, n]
Parent / children O(1) g >> 1, 2g + {0,1}²
Interpolated query O(1) grid_sample per level + blend
Recentre by Δ cells O(n·Δ) with offsets; O(n²) with torch.roll start with roll (recentring happens every ~0.2–1 s), switch to offsets if profiling says so
Decay O(touched cells) lazy, via t_last
Serialise hollow rings O(n²·L) mask the inner quarter of levels ≥ 1

Cache behaviour on CPU is good (contiguous rows); on GPU everything is a dense tensor kernel.

12.3 Why not the alternatives

A pointer quadtree has unpredictable memory, poor cache locality and no GPU path. A linear quadtree (Morton-keyed) fixes locality but still needs a sort or hash per frame, and its layout changes whenever content changes, which complicates temporal fusion. A polar grid matches the sensor but must be resampled every time the vehicle translates, which is exactly the aliasing the brief asks to avoid. A spatial hash is only used for the optional refinement tiles.

13Section 13: 3D → 2.5D projection

13.1 One lattice for all levels

Given a point p in the map frame M (float64 arithmetic for the floor):
    g   = floor(p_xy / s₀)                     ∈ ℤ²     fine lattice index
    g_ℓ = floor(g / 2^ℓ)                       ∈ ℤ²     level-ℓ index (arithmetic shift)
    a_ℓ = C · 2^(L−1−ℓ) − n/2                  ∈ ℤ²     window corner, C = centre in coarsest cells
    u_ℓ = g_ℓ − a_ℓ                             valid iff 0 ≤ u_ℓ < n (half-open)
    storage index = (u_ℓ + offset_ℓ) mod n

Exact nesting, proved. floor(floor(x/2^ℓ)/2) = floor(x/2^(ℓ+1)), so the parent of a point's level-ℓ cell is always its level-(ℓ+1) cell. For the windows, a_ℓ = 2·a_{ℓ+1} + n/2, so level ℓ's window occupies exactly cells [n/4, 3n/4)² of level ℓ+1 (integers because n is a multiple of 4). Consequences:

  • No misalignment: every level derives from one quantisation of one number.
  • No gaps or overlaps: with hollow ownership (level ℓ ≥ 1 owns cells outside [n/4, 3n/4)²), the owned regions partition the full extent exactly.
  • No rounding disagreements: all window arithmetic is integer.

13.2 Cell states

State Meaning
UNKNOWN Never observed, or decayed below ε
OBSERVED Has point evidence
INPAINTED Ground height estimated, no direct evidence
FREE (optional layer) A beam passed through at obstacle height
SUSPICIOUS Unobserved drivable patch inside observed drivable surface (possible negative obstacle)

Empty is not free. Points outside the largest window are dropped and counted.

13.3 Recentring

target = snap(p_ego (+ look-ahead), s_{L−1})
if |target − c|∞ ≥ δ:                        δ = 1.6–2.4 m, a multiple of s_{L−1}
    Δ_ℓ = (target − c) / s_ℓ                  integer for every level
    offset_ℓ += Δ_ℓ ; clear newly exposed rows/columns (UNKNOWN)
    c = target

Because the grid is yaw-fixed, rotation of the vehicle never moves cells. Cells leaving the fine window keep their information in coarser levels; cells entering it inherit parent values through the push step until fine evidence arrives, so there is no visual "pop".

13.4 Insertion (vectorised pseudocode)

def insert(clip, P, prob, is_ground, t):
    # P: (N,3) float64 map-frame points; prob: (N,K) fp16; is_ground: (N,) bool
    g = torch.floor(P[:, :2] / clip.s0).long()
    for l in range(clip.L):
        u = torch.div(g, 2**l, rounding_mode="floor") - clip.corner(l)
        m = ((u >= 0) & (u < clip.n)).all(dim=1)
        if not m.any():
            continue
        idx = clip.storage_index(l, u[m])                 # flat index into level l
        clip.decay_touched(l, idx.unique(), t)            # lazy decay, once per cell
        z, gnd, p = P[m, 2].float(), is_ground[m], prob[m]
        clip.Wg[l].index_add_(0, idx[gnd], torch.ones_like(z[gnd]))
        clip.Sg[l].index_add_(0, idx[gnd], z[gnd])
        clip.Qg[l].index_add_(0, idx[gnd], z[gnd] ** 2)
        o = ~gnd
        clip.Wo[l].index_add_(0, idx[o], torch.ones_like(z[o]))
        clip.Zlo[l].scatter_reduce_(0, idx[o], z[o], "amin")
        clip.Zhi[l].scatter_reduce_(0, idx[o], z[o], "amax")
        clip.E[l].index_add_(0, idx, p.float())            # (n*n, K) class evidence
        clip.Tlast[l][idx] = t

A point at 60 m touches only level 3; a point at 5 m touches all four. With your frame (22,816 scene points) this is 84,279 scatter writes per frame.

13.5 Preventing discontinuities and aliasing

Problem Mechanism
Gaps, overlaps, misalignment Single integer lattice; power-of-two nesting; hollow ownership (§13.1)
Inconsistent values across levels Additive statistics inserted into every containing level: a coarse cell is the exact merge of its children
Aliasing Box-filter aggregation over all points (never pick one point per cell); max for obstacles; no per-frame resampling (yaw-fixed grid, integer scrolling)
Seams in derived layers (slope, step) Ghost cells: neighbours outside a level's window are read from level ℓ+1 by bilinear interpolation
Seams in continuous queries Blend band of width w_ℓ = 4·s_{ℓ+1} inside each window edge (below)
Pops when the fovea moves Push-down inheritance from the parent level, flagged INPAINTED
Loss of thin/small obstacles max/any aggregation + geometric obstacle fallback + object list

Continuous query (visualisation, planners that sample arbitrary points):

d  = |x − c|∞ ;  ℓ₀ = finest level with d < E_ℓ₀
α  = clamp( (d − (E_ℓ₀ − w_ℓ₀)) / w_ℓ₀ , 0, 1 )
v(x) = (1 − α) · bilerp_ℓ₀(x) + α · bilerp_{ℓ₀+1}(x)          continuous layers
class(x) = argmax_k [ (1 − α) · E_k,ℓ₀(x) + α · E_k,ℓ₀+1(x) ]   categorical layers (blend evidence, not labels)

13.6 What is lost, and where

Horizontal position within a cell (≤ s_ℓ/√2), the vertical distribution beyond three heights, multiple vertical gaps (two overhangs in one cell), and per-point intensity. §26 measures each of these.

14Section 14: What each cell stores

Two separate things live in a cell: accumulators (mergeable statistics that fusion updates) and products (derived layers that consumers read). Products can be recomputed from accumulators at any time, so they never need to be fused themselves.

14.1 Core representation (minimum useful): 12 bytes per cell

Layer Type Bytes Notes
Ground elevation ĥ int16, cm 2 Relative to the map's z anchor (±327 m)
Obstacle bottom (clearance reference) int16, cm 2 Lowest non-ground point
Obstacle top int16, cm 2 Highest non-ground point
Point weight uint16, saturating 2 Evidence strength
Class uint8 1 Argmax of evidence
Confidence uint8 1 max E / ΣE × 255
Traversability uint8 1 0–253 cost, 254 lethal, 255 unknown
Flags uint8 1 observed, inpainted, dynamic, suspicious, free, stale

14.2 Extended representation: +36 bytes (48 bytes per cell)

Layer Type Bytes
Ground and obstacle weights (decayed) float16 × 2 4
Σz, Σz² of ground points float32 × 2 8
Class evidence E_k (K = 10) uint8 × 10 (log-scaled) 10
Elevation standard deviation uint8 (log-quantised, mm) 1
Slope x, y int8 × 2 2
Roughness uint8 1
Step height uint8 (cm) 1
Mean intensity uint8 1
Last update time uint16 (×10 ms, wraps) 2
Velocity x, y (optional) int8 × 2 (0.25 m/s) 2
Track ID (optional) uint16 2
Reserved / alignment — 2

Keep accumulators in float32 on the GPU during processing (quantise only for storage and transmission). Per-cell velocity is optional because velocity is better represented in the object list; it exists so that a planner reading only the grid still sees motion.

14.3 Memory for the whole map

Layout Cells Core (12 B) Extended (48 B)
Clipmap 4 × 512, stored (all levels full) 1,048,576 12.0 MiB 48.0 MiB
Clipmap 4 × 512, owned cells only (hollow) 851,968 9.8 MiB 39.0 MiB
Two-level 5 cm / 40 cm (brief's pattern) 520,192 6.0 MiB 23.8 MiB
Circular 5 cm (r < 10 m) + 50 cm (to 100 m), not alignable ≈ 250,070 2.9 MiB 11.4 MiB
Uniform 5 cm, ±102.4 m 16,777,216 192 MiB 768 MiB
Uniform 10 cm 4,194,304 48 MiB 192 MiB
Uniform 20 cm 1,048,576 12 MiB 48 MiB
Uniform 40 cm 262,144 3 MiB 12 MiB

The clipmap costs the same as a uniform 20 cm grid but is 4× finer near the vehicle and 2× coarser far away, and 16× (stored) to 19.7× (owned) smaller than uniform 5 cm. In general:

N_owned = n² · (1 + 3(L−1)/4)                  grows with log(range)
N_uniform(s₀) = (n · 2^(L−1))²                   grows with range²
ratio = 4^(L−1) / (1 + 3(L−1)/4)               = 19.7 for L = 4, 64 for L = 5

15Section 15: Aggregation

Quantity Statistic Mergeable? Why
Ground elevation Mean of ground-labelled points (with outlier gate) Yes (Σz, w) Unbiased; sensor noise averages out
Ground spread Variance (Σz², Σz, w) Yes Roughness and uncertainty
Ground lowest point Minimum Yes Depressions
Obstacle top Maximum Yes Conservative; poles and thin objects survive coarse cells
Obstacle bottom Minimum of non-ground points Yes Overhang clearance
Obstacle presence Weight (count) > threshold, any rule near the car Yes A single return can be a real obstacle
Class Sum of probabilities (evidence) → argmax Yes Soft voting; resists single mislabelled points
Confidence max E / ΣE Derived Calibrated-ish vote share
Intensity Mean Yes Lane markings (only valid at fine levels)
Median, percentiles — No Cannot be merged exactly across cells or time; use variance gating instead
Learned aggregation (per-cell MLP) — No Breaks exact cross-level consistency; research ablation only

Effects to expect:

  • Terrain: the mean of ground-only points is accurate; a mean over all points (a common shortcut) lifts the ground at every pole, car and curb. This is the main reason for the two-height design.
  • Obstacles: max keeps a 10 cm pole visible in a 40 cm cell; mean would erase it.
  • Boundaries: a cell straddling a car edge takes the obstacle's top and the ground's mean, so the footprint grows by up to one cell. That dilation is conservative and bounded by s_ℓ, and it is measured by the boundary F-score in §26.
  • Elevation accuracy: limited by ground-point count per cell; coarse cells average more points and are therefore less noisy but more biased on curved ground (bias ≈ κ·s²/24 per axis for curvature κ).
  • Semantics: evidence voting favours the majority class in mixed cells; thin classes are protected by the geometric obstacle fallback, not by the vote.

16Section 16: Distant objects

16.1 How many points does a distant object get?

For a surface of width w and height h facing the sensor,

N(r) ≈ (w · h) / (r² · Δφ · Δθ)
Pedestrian (0.6 × 1.7 m) 10 m 20 m 50 m 100 m
Your sim (0.16° × 0.4°) ≈ 520 ≈ 130 ≈ 21 ≈ 5
0.16° × 0.2° ≈ 1,050 ≈ 260 ≈ 42 ≈ 10
128-beam class (0.1° × 0.1°) ≈ 3,350 ≈ 840 ≈ 134 ≈ 33

The model is an upper bound (the pedestrian in your frame at 10 m has 299 points). Occlusion makes it worse: your bicycle at 27 m has 4 points because a truck hides it.

16.2 Policy

  1. Never average away sparse evidence. Obstacle presence uses max/any; no kNN outlier filter online.
  2. Detection runs on points, not on the map. A 5-point pedestrian at 100 m is a detection problem, and the map cannot help it.
  3. Objects keep full precision. The object list stores boxes in continuous coordinates at every range; the 40 cm grid only holds their footprint.
  4. Range-aware thresholds. Detection score thresholds and minimum point counts are set per distance band from validation curves.
  5. Temporal confirmation instead of spatial filtering. Far detections become tracks after 2 hits; far single-return cells are confirmed by persistence.
  6. Unknown is not free. Cells behind objects and beyond the last return stay UNKNOWN, and the planner must treat them as such.
  7. Resolution should not increase for distant objects. Refining cells beyond the sampling density adds no information; semantic or risk importance is expressed through the object list and priority. The only justified increase is the optional refinement along azimuth where Δ_h(r) is still smaller than s_ℓ (§11.3).
  8. Report accuracy per distance band. This is the metric the brief asks for.

17Section 17: Memory and computation analysis

17.1 Assumptions

10 Hz sensor; ±102.4 m square map; 8 m height band for 3D voxels; typical 64-beam scan ≈ 120 k points × 16 B (xyz + intensity); 128-beam scan ≈ 262 k points × 20 B (with time); your organised frame 227,351 × 7 × 4 B.

17.2 Per-frame size and bandwidth

Representation Size per frame 10 Hz stream
Raw 64-beam scan 1.83 MiB 154 Mbit/s
Raw 128-beam scan 5.0 MiB 419 Mbit/s
Your organised frame, binary 6.07 MiB (6.5 MB as ASCII) 509 Mbit/s
Dense 3D voxels, 5 cm, 1 byte 2.5 GiB not transmittable
Dense 3D voxels, 5 cm, 1 bit 320 MiB not transmittable
Sparse accumulated 3D voxels, 5 cm (estimate: 5–10 M surface voxels × ~32 B incl. hash overhead) 150–300 MiB not transmittable
Uniform 2.5D 5 cm, core 192 MiB 1.6 Gbit/s
Clipmap, core, full 12.0 MiB 1.0 Gbit/s
Clipmap, cells touched this frame, sparse (index + 12 B) 0.24 MiB on your frame (15,812 cells) ≈ 20 Mbit/s before compression

The honest conclusion: a dense map is not smaller than one scan. The clipmap is 200× smaller than a dense 5 cm 3D grid and 16× smaller than a uniform 5 cm 2.5D grid, but its value over raw points is different: fixed size regardless of drive length, O(1) queries, fused over time, labelled, and ready for a planner. Transmit deltas (touched cells) with zstd, not full frames.

17.3 Computation per frame

Step Work Order of magnitude
Preprocess O(N) transforms 10⁵–10⁶ flops
Voxelise O(N log N) unique several ms on CPU, about 1 ms on GPU
Sparse conv layer ≈ V · K_eff · C_in · C_out; V = 10⁵ voxels, K_eff ≈ 10 active neighbours, C = 32 → 10⁹ mult-adds per full-resolution layer Dominant cost
Grid insert N · L̄ scatter writes (84,279 on your frame) < 1 ms on GPU
Derived layers ~20 ops × L · n² = 2 × 10⁷ 1–3 ms on GPU
Visibility clearing obstacle cells × 9 pixel reads < 1 ms on GPU
Uniform 5 cm equivalent derived pass ~20 ops × 16.8 M cells = 3.4 × 10⁸ 16× the clipmap cost

18Section 18: Real-time architecture

18.1 Targets

Platform Input rate End-to-end latency target Notes
Workstation (RTX 4080/4090 class) 10 Hz mean ≤ 60 ms, p99 ≤ 100 ms Full model, FP16
Edge (Jetson AGX Orin) 10 Hz p99 ≤ 100 ms TensorRT, reduced width, possibly L = 3 or n = 384

"FPS" is reported as sustained throughput without drops, plus latency percentiles. All numbers below are budgets to verify, not measurements.

18.2 Latency budget (workstation)

Stage Budget
Ingest (binary) + validity 2 ms
Preprocess (ego filter, deskew, level, crop) 3 ms
Voxelise 2 ms
Network (FP16) 25–40 ms
Post-processing (argmax, devoxelise, peaks/NMS) 3 ms
Tracking 2 ms
Grid scroll + insert + decay 4 ms
Clearing + terrain derivation 5 ms
Publish (delta, zstd) 3 ms
Total ≈ 50–65 ms
Visualisation outside the loop, 2–5 Hz

18.3 Execution model

  • One CUDA stream in the main loop; pinned host buffers and non-blocking copies.
  • Latest-wins input queue: if a scan arrives while the previous one is still processing, the older queued scan is dropped. Latency must never accumulate.
  • The visualiser runs in another process so that rendering a million cells can never stall perception.
  • Later optimisation: run decay and clearing on a second CUDA stream in parallel with inference (they only need the range image and the previous map).

18.4 Likely bottlenecks, in expected order

  1. ASCII point-cloud parsing (seconds per frame; convert offline).
  2. Python loops over points or cells (must be vectorised from day one).
  3. Host ↔ device copies of point arrays (keep data on the GPU from voxelisation to map).
  4. Sparse convolutions (FP16, TensorRT/libspconv, channel width).
  5. unique() calls (sort-based); replace with hashing kernels if they show up.
  6. Full-map derived recomputation (restrict to dirty tiles).
  7. Visualisation serialisation (decimate, send deltas).

20Section 20: Hardware

Role CPU GPU RAM Storage Notes
Development 8–16 cores ≥ 16 GB VRAM (RTX 4080 class) 64 GB 2 TB NVMe Runs the whole pipeline in real time
Training 16–32 cores (data loading) 1–4 × 24–48 GB (RTX 4090, RTX 6000 Ada, L40S, A100) 128 GB 4 TB NVMe + bulk HDD/NAS SemanticKITTI ≈ 80 GB raw; nuScenes full set several hundred GB (LiDAR-only subsets are smaller)

MATLAB simulation 8+ cores optional (needed for Unreal-based simulation) 32 GB 500 GB Windows for Unreal co-simulation

Networking on a vehicle: 1 GbE per LiDAR (a 128-beam sensor needs ~0.4 Gbit/s), 10 GbE for logging, PTP time synchronisation.

Can it all run on the edge? Yes, with compromises: FP16/INT8 TensorRT; backbone width ×0.5 or a range-image backbone; 10 cm voxels (never 5 cm); L = 3 (±51.2 m) or n = 384 if memory bandwidth is tight; detection at 5 Hz while semantics and mapping run at 10 Hz; visualisation off-board; grid engine as CUDA kernels in C++. Expect a few mIoU points of loss; measure it (§36).

21Section 21: Dataset strategy

21.1 Public datasets

Dataset LiDAR Labels relevant here Sequences / poses Diversity Licence Fit for this project
SemanticKITTI 1 × HDL-64E, 10 Hz Dense per-point semantics (road, sidewalk, parking, terrain, pole, building, fence, vegetation, vehicles, persons), moving vs static labels 22 sequences, poses One city, dry weather CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 Primary real benchmark for semantics, terrain classes and moving objects
nuScenes (+ lidarseg) 1 × HDL-32E, 20 Hz Per-point semantics on keyframes (drivable surface, sidewalk, terrain, manmade, vegetation…), 3D boxes with velocity, tracking 1000 scenes, ego poses Boston and Singapore, rain, night CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (commercial licence available) Secondary: detection, tracking, sparse sensor, weather
Waymo Open (Perception) 5 LiDARs (top unit 64-beam, 75 m) 3D boxes; segmentation on a subset 20 s segments, poses Several US cities Custom non-commercial Optional long-range check; heavy preprocessing
KITTI-360 HDL-64E + push-broom Dense accumulated 3D semantics and instances Long sequences, poses One city CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 Optional elevation / static map ground truth
Argoverse 2 (Sensor) 2 × VLP-32C 3D boxes, tracking; HD map with drivable area and a dense ground-height raster 1000 scenarios, poses Six US cities CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 Optional ground-height and drivable-area ground truth in BEV
RELLIS-3D Ouster OS1-64 Off-road semantics (grass, mud, rubble…) Sequences Off-road only CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 Optional: non-drivable terrain generalisation
SemanticPOSS 40-beam Dense pedestrians and riders Small Campus Research Optional: crowded scenes
