Check every licence against your intended use; nearly all are non-commercial.

21.2 Recommended strategy

  1. Development and correctness: your MATLAB simulation (exact labels, poses and geometry; small and fast).
  2. Main training and benchmark: SemanticKITTI (sequences 00–07, 09–10 train; 08 validation, the standard split).
  3. Detection, tracking, sparse sensor, weather: nuScenes (fine-tune the same backbone).
  4. Map-level ground truth: accumulated static labelled points (SemanticKITTI with poses, KITTI-360) and simulation meshes.
  5. Controlled distance and occlusion studies: MATLAB scenario sweeps (§21.6).
  6. Sim-to-real: pre-train on simulation + real mixture; always report real-data results separately.

21.3 Ground truth for the map

For each evaluation frame, build a reference raster at 5 cm by accumulating labelled static points from frames t−N … t+N (N ≈ 20–50) using the poses, excluding moving points, and taking per-cell ground mean and obstacle max. Mark reference cells with fewer than m points as "no reference". In simulation, rasterise the road mesh for exact ground elevation and actor boxes for exact footprints.

21.4 Your MATLAB / Simulink data: what it is good for

Strength Use it for
Exact per-point class and instance labels, exact poses, exact object boxes and velocities Testing the grid engine against ground truth; oracle-semantics experiments
Full control of sensor parameters Sensor sweeps: 16–128 beams, 0.1–0.4° resolution, 30–120 m range, mount height; measure how the best level schedule moves
Scripted placement of objects Distance ladders: the same pedestrian at 5, 10 … 100 m and at several bearings; clean accuracy-vs-distance curves
Controlled occlusion Targets behind trucks with varied overlap (your bicycle case)
Repeatable dynamics Crossing pedestrians, overtakes, cut-ins for tracking and motion state
Weakness Mitigation
Flat roads, no off-road ground, no curbs or potholes in this export Build terrain scenes in RoadRunner (curbs, sidewalks, grades, banking) and run them with the Unreal Engine-based lidar block, which can also output labels (check your release and licence); or use CARLA
Simple object meshes, no vegetation or buildings Use real datasets for semantic diversity
Unrealistic intensity (near-perfect class cue) Train without intensity, or randomise it
Idealised noise and no motion distortion Enable noise; add dropout and jitter augmentation; test deskew on real data
Uniform beam spacing Choose limits and resolution close to your target sensor

21.5 Fix the export first

Change your exporter so that simulated and real data share one loader. Adopt a SemanticKITTI-compatible layout with the organised shape preserved:

sim_root/sequences/<seq>/
  velodyne/000000.bin     float32, H·W × 4, row-major (x, y, z, intensity), NaN = no return
  labels/000000.label     uint32,  H·W, (instance << 16) | class_id, 0 = no return
  poses.txt               12 numbers per line: T_world_sensor (3×4, row-major)
  times.txt               seconds per frame
  objects/000000.json     actor id, class, centre, size, yaw, velocity (world frame)
  meta.yaml               H, W, elevation and azimuth tables, sensor mount, class map, ego actor id
  road_mesh.ply           road surface in world frame (elevation ground truth)

Specific fixes for your current files: write binary instead of ASCII (≈ 25× smaller and ~100× faster to read); store IDs as unsigned integers (your road ID is already corrupted by float32); remap actor IDs to compact 16-bit instance IDs with a saved lookup table; drop material_id or populate it; record the ego actor ID; export ego pose and sensor mount every frame; raise MaxRange to 120 m.

21.6 Export script sketch (MATLAB)

Adapt names to the code that Driving Scenario Designer generates for your scenario (Export → MATLAB Function shows the exact sensor constructor and call signature for your release).

[scenario, ego] = createMyScenario();                  % exported from Driving Scenario Designer
lidar = lidarPointCloudGenerator('SensorIndex',1, 'UpdateInterval',0.1, ...
    'SensorLocation',[1.5 0], 'Height',1.6, 'MaxRange',120, ...
    'AzimuthResolution',0.16, 'AzimuthLimits',[-180 180], ...
    'ElevationResolution',0.4, 'ElevationLimits',[-25 15], ...
    'HasNoise',true, 'HasOrganizedOutput',true, 'HasEgoVehicle',true, ...
    'HasRoadsInputPort',true, 'ActorProfiles',actorProfiles(scenario));

out = fullfile('sim_root','sequences','0000');
for d = ["velodyne","labels","objects"], mkdir(fullfile(out,d)); end
fPose = fopen(fullfile(out,'poses.txt'),'w'); fTime = fopen(fullfile(out,'times.txt'),'w');
idMap = containers.Map('KeyType','double','ValueType','double');   % actor id -> instance id
k = 0;
while advance(scenario)
    t = scenario.SimulationTime;
    [pc, ok, clusters] = lidar(targetPoses(ego), roadMesh(ego, lidar.MaxRange), t);
    if ~ok, continue; end

    xyz = single(pc.Location);                                    % H x W x 3
    I = zeros(size(xyz,1), size(xyz,2), 'single');
    if ~isempty(pc.Intensity), I = single(pc.Intensity); end
    writeRowMajor(fullfile(out,'velodyne',sprintf('%06d.bin',k)), cat(3,xyz,I), 'single');

    cls  = uint32(clusters(:,:,2));
    act  = double(clusters(:,:,1));
    [u, ~, j] = unique(act);                                      % map each distinct actor once
    ids  = arrayfun(@(a) instanceId(idMap, a), u);
    inst = uint32(reshape(ids(j), size(act)));
    writeRowMajor(fullfile(out,'labels',sprintf('%06d.label',k)), bitor(cls, bitshift(inst,16)), 'uint32');

    T = worldFromSensor(ego, lidar);                              % 4 x 4 double
    fprintf(fPose, '%.9f ', reshape(T(1:3,:).', 1, [])); fprintf(fPose, '\n');
    fprintf(fTime, '%.6f\n', t);
    writeObjects(fullfile(out,'objects',sprintf('%06d.json',k)), scenario, ego);  % jsonencode actor poses + dimensions
    k = k + 1;
end
fclose(fPose); fclose(fTime);

function writeRowMajor(file, A, type)
    % MATLAB is column-major; reverse dimension order so the byte stream is row-major (H, W, C)
    A = permute(A, ndims(A):-1:1);
    fid = fopen(file,'w'); fwrite(fid, A, type); fclose(fid);
end

function id = instanceId(map, actor)
    if actor == 0 || actor > 1e6, id = 0; return; end             % no return, or road / static mesh
    if ~isKey(map, actor), map(actor) = map.Count + 1; end        % handle object: updates persist
    id = map(actor);
end

function T = worldFromSensor(ego, lidar)
    Rz = @(a)[cosd(a) -sind(a) 0; sind(a) cosd(a) 0; 0 0 1];
    Ry = @(a)[cosd(a) 0 sind(a); 0 1 0; -sind(a) 0 cosd(a)];
    Rx = @(a)[1 0 0; 0 cosd(a) -sind(a); 0 sind(a) cosd(a)];
    Tw = [Rz(ego.Yaw)*Ry(ego.Pitch)*Rx(ego.Roll), ego.Position(:); 0 0 0 1];      % world <- vehicle
    Ts = [Rz(lidar.Yaw)*Ry(lidar.Pitch)*Rx(lidar.Roll), [lidar.SensorLocation(:); lidar.Height]; 0 0 0 1];
    T  = Tw * Ts;                           % world <- sensor (check sign conventions once with a known pose)
end

Save the ID lookup table (idMap) and the class specification into meta.yaml at the end. Validate the export with the Python loader: the road must sit at z ≈ −Height in the sensor frame, and poses.txt must reproduce the ego trajectory.

The Python side, until the exporter is updated, can read your current files directly:

def read_matlab_pcd(path):
    hdr, n_hdr = {}, 0
    with open(path) as f:
        for n_hdr, line in enumerate(f, 1):
            key, *val = line.split()
            if not key.startswith("#"): hdr[key] = val
            if key == "DATA": break
    W, H = int(hdr["WIDTH"][0]), int(hdr["HEIGHT"][0])
    a = np.loadtxt(path, skiprows=n_hdr, dtype=np.float64)      # slow: convert once, then cache
    a = a.reshape(W, H, -1).transpose(1, 0, 2)                  # MATLAB column-major -> (H, W, C)
    fields = hdr["FIELDS"]
    return {name: a[..., i] for i, name in enumerate(fields)}   # ids kept as float64 here only

21.7 Scenario matrix for experiments

Family Variables Measures
Distance ladder class ∈ {pedestrian, cyclist, car, pole, barrier}; range 5–100 m step 5; bearing 0°, ±30°, ±90° Detection recall, semantic IoU, map obstacle recall vs distance
Occlusion occluder size; overlap 0–90 % Recall under occlusion; unknown-cell handling
Terrain (RoadRunner) curb 5/10/15/20 cm; grade 0–15 %; banking; ramps; kerb-side parking Elevation, step and slope error by level
Dynamics speed 0–15 m/s; crossing angle; cut-ins Tracking, motion state, ghost removal
Sensor sweep beams, resolutions, range, height Fill ratio, fidelity, best n and L
Ego motion 0–25 m/s Temporal fill of the fovea; recentring behaviour

21.8 Live streaming from Simulink

For real-time demos, drive the pipeline from Simulink: Scenario Reader → Lidar Point Cloud Generator → ROS 2 publisher (ROS Toolbox, sensor_msgs/PointCloud2 plus a pose message) → the pipeline's ROS 2 adapter. Without ROS Toolbox, a UDP sender with the same binary frame layout works. The pipeline code does not change; only the reader does.

22Section 22: Training pipeline

22.1 Data preparation

  1. Convert every source to the common frame layout (§21.5); verify with data-validation tests (§34).
  2. Map labels to the project taxonomy with per-dataset lookup tables; unmapped classes fail the build.
  3. Build auxiliary targets offline: 40 cm ground-height rasters from accumulated ground points (SemanticKITTI, KITTI-360, sim meshes); box lists (nuScenes, sim); moving flags.
  4. Store splits as manifests (sequence, frame, checksum). Voxelisation happens on the fly on the GPU, so no voxel cache is needed.

22.2 Augmentation

Augmentation Purpose
Global yaw (full 360°), flip, scale 0.95–1.05, small translation Rotation invariance (required by the map-aligned input frame)
Beam dropout (remove every k-th row of the organised scan) Generalise across 32/64/128-beam sensors and your simulated sensor
Point dropout, range-dependent jitter Noise robustness
Intensity jitter or removal Stop the model relying on intensity; essential for sim-to-real
Scene mixing (LaserMix, PolarMix) Established gains for LiDAR segmentation
Object copy-paste (instance sampling), including at long range Rare classes, distant pedestrians and cyclists
Sim–real mixing (e.g. 20–30 % simulated scans) Use exact simulated labels without overfitting to them

22.3 Losses

L_sem = CE(weighted, w_c = 1 / ln(1.02 + f_c)) + Lovász-softmax            ignore class 0
L_gnd = mask · ( |h − ĥ|² / (2σ²) + ½·log σ² ) + BCE(valid)                 heteroscedastic
L_det = GaussianFocal(heatmap) + 0.25 · L1(offset, z, log-dims, sin/cos yaw, velocity)
L_mov = BCE(moving, pos_weight)                                             optional
L     = L_sem + λ_g · L_gnd + λ_d · L_det + λ_m · L_mov                     λ tuned on validation

Mixed-dataset batches only apply the losses for which a sample has labels (SemanticKITTI: semantics, moving, ground; nuScenes: semantics on keyframes, boxes; simulation: everything).

22.4 Schedule

Stage Data Heads Goal
A SemanticKITTI Semantics Reproduce a known sparse U-Net result within a few mIoU points
B SemanticKITTI (+ KITTI-360) + ground height Ground regression without hurting semantics
C nuScenes + objects Detection head on the shared backbone
D Mixed All Joint fine-tune
E Mixed + simulation All Sim transfer; test on held-out simulated scenarios

Stage letters follow the heads' training dependencies. The roadmap (§31) runs stage B after stage C, because the ground head is only worth adding once the pull–push baseline exists to compare against.

Defaults to start from (then tune): AdamW, one-cycle learning rate peaking at 2e-3, weight decay 0.01, 30–50 epochs, batch 4–8 scans, mixed precision, gradient clipping at 10, EMA of weights optional. Hyperparameter search: small grids (learning rate, voxel size, width) on 20 % of the data with short schedules, then one full run per finalist.

22.5 Validation, checkpoints, export

  • Validate every epoch on a fixed subset, full validation at the end; log per-class and distance-binned IoU.
  • Keep last, best-mIoU and, later, best-composite (weighted semantic + detection score). Each checkpoint bundles the config, taxonomy, voxel size, git hash and dataset manifest hash.
  • Export: dense parts to ONNX, sparse backbone through NVIDIA's sparse-conv TensorRT path; a parity test must show per-point argmax agreement ≥ 99.5 % against PyTorch FP32 on a fixed set.

23Section 23: Inference pipeline

RawScan ─► preprocess ─► PointBatch ─► network ─► PerceptionOut ─► tracker ─► tracks
                                                     │                          │
pose ────► map recentre ───────────────────────────► grid insert ◄──────────────┘
                                                     ▼
                                      fusion, decay, clearing ─► terrain derivation
                                                     ▼
                                     MapSnapshot (+ tracks) ─► publisher / visualiser / metrics

23.1 Interfaces

@dataclass
class RawScan:                      # produced by any reader (file, sensor, ROS 2, Simulink)
    stamp_ns: int
    xyz: np.ndarray                 # (H, W, 3) or (N, 3) float32, sensor frame, NaN = invalid
    intensity: np.ndarray | None    # same leading shape
    t_offset: np.ndarray | None     # seconds since stamp
    rowcol: np.ndarray | None       # (N, 2) int16 when unorganised
    sensor: SensorSpec              # beams, resolutions, extrinsic T_base_sensor

@dataclass
class PointBatch:                   # on device after preprocessing
    xyz: torch.Tensor               # (N, 3) float32, map frame, relative to map anchor
    feats: torch.Tensor             # (N, F)
    rowcol: torch.Tensor | None     # (N, 2)
    stamp_ns: int
    T_map_base: torch.Tensor        # (4, 4) float64

@dataclass
class PerceptionOut:
    cls_topk: torch.Tensor          # (N, 3) uint8
    prob_topk: torch.Tensor         # (N, 3) float16
    moving: torch.Tensor | None     # (N,) float16
    ground_bev: torch.Tensor | None # (3, 512, 512): height, log sigma, valid (map lattice, level 3)
    boxes: torch.Tensor | None      # (M, 11): x y z l w h yaw vx vy score class

@dataclass
class MapSnapshot:
    stamp_ns: int
    center: tuple[int, int]         # in coarsest-cell units
    spec: GridSpec                  # s0, L, n, layer schema
    layers: dict[str, torch.Tensor] # each (L, n, n) or (L, n, n, C)
    tracks: list[Track]
    health: HealthFlags             # pose missing, model fallback, latency overrun ...

Every stage is a pure function of its inputs plus explicit state (Clipmap, Tracker), which makes replay, testing and benchmarking deterministic.

24Section 24: Software architecture

24.1 Modules

Module Responsibility Depends on
core Data types, transforms, timing, registry —
io Readers/writers: PCD, KITTI-style, MATLAB exports, nuScenes, MCAP core
datasets Training datasets, label maps, augmentations io, core
preprocess Ego filter, crop, deskew, levelling, range image core
models Voxeliser, backbones, heads, losses, multi-task wrapper core
perception Inference wrapper, post-processing, clustering, box decoding models
grid GridSpec protocol; Clipmap, UniformGrid, PolarGrid; accumulators; queries; serialisation core
terrain Ground baseline, pull–push, features, traversability grid
temporal Odometry adapters, fusion/decay, visibility clearing, tracking grid, core
pipeline Stage composition, sync and async runners, health all online modules
viz Rerun logging, colour maps, comparison views grid, core
eval Metrics, GT builders, distance binning, reports grid, io
ros2 (later) Thin adapter nodes pipeline

Tightly coupled: voxeliser + backbone + heads (one versioned unit); grid + terrain derivation (shared tensors). Independent: readers, tracker, visualiser, evaluation, ROS adapter. The grid engine never imports the model; it consumes points and probabilities, which is what allows oracle-label experiments.

24.2 Key abstractions

class GridEngine(Protocol):
    spec: GridSpec
    def recenter(self, T_map_base: torch.Tensor) -> None: ...
    def insert(self, xyz: torch.Tensor, prob: torch.Tensor, cls: torch.Tensor,
               is_ground: torch.Tensor, stamp: float) -> None: ...
    def clear_visible(self, range_image: torch.Tensor, T_map_sensor: torch.Tensor) -> None: ...
    def derive(self, ground_prior: torch.Tensor | None = None) -> None: ...
    def query(self, xy: torch.Tensor, layer: str, blend: bool = True) -> torch.Tensor: ...
    def snapshot(self, owned_only: bool = False) -> MapSnapshot: ...
    def memory_bytes(self, owned_only: bool = False) -> int: ...

Uniform, two-level, polar and clipmap grids all implement this protocol, so every baseline is a configuration switch.

24.3 Configuration, logging, errors, models, experiments

  • Configuration: Hydra groups sensor/, dataset/, grid/, model/, pipeline/, train/, eval/; structured dataclass configs validate types at start-up; every run writes its fully resolved config.
  • Logging: Python logging with JSON output; one record per frame with stage timings, counts and health flags; NVTX ranges mirror the stage names.
  • Error handling (fail-soft, never silent): missing pose → skip fusion, publish single-scan map with a flag; model failure or timeout → geometric fallback (Patchwork++ + height rules) with a flag; NaN or infinite values → dropped and counted; latency overrun → drop the next queued scan and raise a health flag.
  • Model management: a registry file maps model names to checkpoint paths, SHA-256, taxonomy version and voxel size; the pipeline refuses mismatched taxonomies.
  • Experiment management: one Hydra output directory and one MLflow run per experiment; results in Parquet; a script regenerates every table and figure from stored results.

25Section 25: Visualisation

Tool: Rerun for development (timeline scrubbing, 3D, 2D, plots, recordings you can share); Foxglove later if ROS 2 is adopted; MATLAB remains useful for checking your exports.

View Content
3D: raw Points coloured by intensity or range; ego box
3D: semantic Points coloured by predicted class; errors (prediction ≠ label) highlighted
3D: map Cell centres as points with radius s_ℓ/2 at ground height, coloured by class; or a height-field mesh per level
3D: objects Boxes with class, track ID and velocity arrows
3D: level borders Line strips for each level's window; optional cell grid for level 0 near the car
2D: BEV layers Class, elevation, obstacle height, clearance, slope, step, traversability, confidence, state (observed / inpainted / unknown)
2D: level map Each cell coloured by its level: shows the fovea directly
2D: range image Organised scan with labels (like the figure above)
Plots Stage latencies, p50/p95, dropped frames, GPU memory, cell counts, bytes per frame
Comparison Uniform 5 cm, clipmap and uniform 40 cm side by side with identical colour maps, per-cell error vs ground truth, and memory annotated

To make the uniform-vs-foveated difference visible, render every grid into the same 5 cm display canvas with nearest-neighbour upsampling (so blockiness is shown honestly, not smoothed), overlay cell borders, and show the error map beside each. A live Pareto plot (bytes vs error) updated per sequence ties the visuals to the numbers.

The visualiser receives decimated snapshots from a separate process at 2–5 Hz, so it cannot slow perception.

26Section 26: Evaluation framework

All map metrics are computed by querying each representation at the same reference points (the 5 cm reference lattice and the original LiDAR points), so grids with different cells are compared fairly. Every metric is also reported per distance band: 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–50, 50–70, 70–100 m.

26.1 Perception

Metric Definition
mIoU, per-class IoU Standard, on points; also on the three groups (terrain / static / movable)
Drivable-surface IoU Points and BEV
Moving-object IoU SemanticKITTI moving-object protocol
Detection AP nuScenes centre-distance thresholds (0.5, 1, 2, 4 m) and BEV IoU; per distance band
Tracking AMOTA, MOTA, ID switches (or HOTA)
Ground segmentation Point precision, recall, F1

26.2 Representation

Metric Definition
Ground elevation error MAE, RMSE, p95 of the absolute error ĥ(query) − h_ref; separately for observed and inpainted cells
Step / curb Step-height error; curb localisation error (m); detection F1
Slope error Degrees
Obstacle recall Share of reference obstacle points (> 0.15 m above ground) whose query cell is marked obstacle
False obstacle rate Share of reference free ground cells marked obstacle
Thin / small object recall Obstacle recall restricted to poles and pedestrians
Boundary F-score Obstacle–free boundary agreement within tolerance τ = 0.1 / 0.25 / 0.5 m
Clearance error For overhang cells
BEV semantic IoU Per class, on the reference lattice
Point envelope consistency Share of input points whose z lies inside the queried [ground, obstacle top] envelope ± tolerance (information retained per point)
Cell purity Share of points in a cell agreeing with the cell's class (aggregation loss)
Seam metric Mean absolute height difference across level-boundary edges divided by the same quantity across interior edges (≈ 1 means no seam)
Coverage Share of reference cells observed / inpainted / unknown

26.3 Efficiency

Bytes (formula and measured VRAM/RSS), cells, insert time, derive time, query time, bytes per frame transmitted (delta + zstd), latency p50/p95/p99 per stage, sustained throughput, dropped frames, energy per frame on Jetson (tegrastats).

26.4 System level

End-to-end latency from sensor timestamp to snapshot publication; CPU and GPU utilisation; scaling with point count (sim beam sweep), with range (30/60/100/150 m) and with n and L; long-run stability (memory flat over 30 min replays).

26.5 The headline result

A set of rate–distortion (Pareto) curves: x = memory or latency, y = distance-weighted obstacle recall, elevation RMSE and BEV mIoU, one point per representation. The claim "foveated is a better trade-off" holds only if the clipmap sits on or above the uniform-grid frontier, with confidence intervals across sequences.

27Section 27: Baseline comparisons

A foveated grid is only interesting if it beats simple alternatives at the same cost. Wherever possible each baseline implements the same GridEngine protocol (§24.2), so a baseline is a configuration file rather than a separate code base, and every representation is scored with the same queries.

27.1 Representation baselines

ID Baseline Configuration Cells / size What it tests
B0 Raw accumulated points All points of the same temporal window, queried by k-nearest neighbours Grows with time (1.8–6 MiB per scan) Geometric fidelity ceiling
B1a Uniform 5 cm, full range 4096 × 4096 over ±102.4 m 16.8 M cells, 192 MiB core The brute-force answer; 2.5D fidelity ceiling
B1b–d Uniform, equal budget 1024 × 1024 at 5 / 10 / 20 cm, covering ±25.6 / ±51.2 / ±102.4 m 1,048,576 cells each, 12 MiB core The decisive comparison: the clipmap's exact cell budget spent either on short range at high resolution or on long range at low resolution
B1e Uniform 40 cm 512 × 512 262,144 cells Cheap lower bound
B2 Two-level 5 / 40 cm (the brief's literal proposal) 5 cm to ±12.8 m, 40 cm beyond, both 512² 520,192 cells Whether a smooth ladder is worth two extra levels
B3 Polar (log-spaced range) 5 cm Cartesian disc to 2 m, then 2048 azimuth bins × 512 range bins growing 0.77 % per bin to 102.4 m ≈ 1.05 M cells Whether cells aligned with the sensor beat Cartesian cells once ego motion and fusion are included (the polar grid must be resampled every frame, and that cost is counted)
B4 Sparse 3D voxels (OctoMap / VDB-style hash) 10 cm and 5 cm, occupancy + class Measured Value and cost of full 3D
B5 Downsampled points Voxel-grid 20 cm; range-adaptive downsampling to the clipmap's byte budget Matched bytes Whether "just downsample the points" is enough
B6 Single-height elevation map Clipmap geometry, one height layer (max z) Same cells as the proposal Value of the two-height design (curbs, overhangs, poles)
B7 2D semantic/occupancy BEV Clipmap geometry, no heights Same cells Value of elevation at all

27.2 Pipeline baselines

ID Baseline Purpose
G1 Geometry only: Patchwork++ ground + height-threshold obstacles + BEV clustering, into the same clipmap Shows what deep learning adds
G2 Oracle semantics: ground-truth labels into the same clipmap Upper bound; separates representation error from perception error
G3 Learned semantics, single scan, no inpainting Isolates the value of temporal fusion and gap filling
G4 A reference segmentation model from an existing code base (for example Pointcept or OpenPCSeg) Sanity check that the in-house network is competitive
G5 Range-image network (RangeNet++ / CENet class) The lightweight alternative for edge hardware

27.3 Fair comparison protocol

  1. Same inputs. Identical scans, poses, temporal windows and crops for every run.
  2. Same perception. Predictions are computed once and cached (cache/pred/<dataset>/<seq>/<frame>.npz: top-3 probabilities, labels, boxes). Every grid consumes the cache, so grid comparisons contain no model randomness. This is possible because the grid engine never imports the model (§24.1).
  3. Same queries. The 5 cm reference lattice plus the original points, the same distance bands and the same reference-validity mask (§21.3).
  4. Same temporal settings (decay constants, clearing, weight caps) for all grid baselines.
  5. Matched budgets. Compare error at equal bytes and bytes at equal error; report both.
  6. Same hardware and timing method. 50 warm-up frames discarded, synchronised GPU timing (§35.2), three repeats, median and p95.
  7. Statistics. Metrics per sequence; 95 % bootstrap confidence intervals over sequences, or over 10 s blocks of frames to respect temporal correlation; paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests between representations on the same frames; three training seeds for anything learned.
  8. Fixed analysis plan. Metric set, bands and headline plots (§26.5) are fixed before the runs, so the conclusion cannot be chosen after seeing the results.

27.4 Experiment set

Experiment Data Inputs Output
E1 Representation fidelity Simulation + SemanticKITTI 08 Oracle labels (G2) into B0–B7 and the proposal Pareto curves free of perception noise
E2 End to end SemanticKITTI 08, nuScenes val Cached predictions The same curves with real perception errors
E3 Efficiency 10 Hz replays All Latency, memory, bytes per frame
E4 Distance and occlusion ladders Simulation (§21.7) Oracle and predicted labels Recall vs distance per representation
E5 Sensor sweep Simulation Oracle labels How the best n, L and s₀ move with beam count and angular resolution

Expected outcome, stated as a hypothesis: the clipmap matches B1a inside 12.8 m, matches B1d beyond 51 m, and dominates B1b–d over the full range at equal memory. If B1c (10 cm to ±51.2 m) matches it on every metric that matters for your use case, the simpler grid wins, and that result should be reported as such.

28Section 28: Ablation studies

Run every ablation with oracle labels first (minutes per run, no training), then repeat only the informative ones with predicted labels. Change one factor at a time from the default configuration, compare pairwise on the same frames, and define a minimum effect worth caring about in advance (for example 1 cm elevation RMSE, 1 mIoU point, 1 % recall) so that a branch can be closed once the confidence interval rules it out.

28.1 Essential

ID Question Variants Main metrics
AB1 Level schedule n ∈ {256, 384, 512, 768}; L ∈ {3, 4, 5}; s₀ ∈ {5, 6.25, 10} cm Elevation RMSE and obstacle recall per band; bytes
AB2 Ground statistic Mean of ground points; mean of all points; min; max Elevation error, step error
AB3 Obstacle statistic Max; mean; count-thresholded max Thin-object recall, false-obstacle rate
AB4 Class statistic Probability evidence; majority vote; last write BEV mIoU, cell purity, label flicker
AB5 Semantic awareness None (geometry only); predicted; oracle Drivable IoU, false obstacles, elevation error near objects
AB6 Height model Two-height; single-height Clearance error, curb error
AB7 Temporal fusion Single scan; accumulate without decay; with decay; decay + clearing; τ × {0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4} Coverage, ghost rate, elevation error
AB8 Gap filling None; pull–push; network ground prior; both with inverse-variance fusion Error on inpainted cells, coverage
AB9 Level transitions Hard switch; blend band; blend band + ghost cells Seam metric, query continuity
AB10 Multi-task learning Semantics only; + ground; + boxes; all heads mIoU, AP, ground error, latency
AB11 Voxel size and width 5 / 10 / 20 cm; width × 0.5 / × 1 mIoU per band, latency, VRAM
AB12 Intensity input With; without; randomised Sim-to-real mIoU gap
AB13 Recentring hysteresis δ ∈ {0, 0.8, 1.6, 2.4} m Recentres per km, pops, latency spikes

28.2 Optional

ID Question Keep it only if
AO1 Velocity look-ahead, τ_la ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 1} s Forward coverage gain outweighs rear loss
AO2 Risk-based refinement tiles (§11.3) It beats distance-only foveation at equal budget near the path
AO3 Finer cells around vulnerable road users Pedestrian footprint error drops measurably
AO4 Learned per-cell aggregation It beats hand-made statistics despite losing exact merges
AO5 Two-sweep network input for motion Moving-object IoU improves at acceptable latency
AO6 Range-image backbone instead of sparse voxels Edge latency gain is worth the accuracy loss
AO7 FP16 / INT8 Parity thresholds hold (§36.2)
AO8 Level factor √2 instead of 2 It shows what exact nesting costs in fidelity
AO9 Circular instead of square level borders Memory saved matters more than scrolling simplicity
AO10 Weight cap w_max Adaptation speed and noise balance improve

29Section 29: Failure modes and mitigations

Several of these are visible in your frame already; they are marked with ◆.

29.1 Sensor and environment

Failure Effect How to detect it Mitigation
Range noise; mixed pixels at object edges Floating points between foreground and background; false obstacles; thick edges Isolated points at depth jumps in the range image Edge filter on range-image depth discontinuities; require ≥ 2 points per obstacle cell except in the near field
Sparsity at range Missed small objects Points per box vs the model in §16.1 Detect on points, temporal confirmation, range-binned thresholds
◆ Near-field blind zone (4.4 m on your sensor) Ground around a stopped car never observed Coverage layer Keep memory from earlier frames; leave cells UNKNOWN, never FREE
◆ Ego self-hits (57 % of your valid points) The car maps itself Points inside the ego box Ego-box crop on real data, ego actor ID in simulation, unit test
◆ Occlusion (your bicycle behind the truck) Unseen space behind objects Ray visibility Explicit UNKNOWN; clear only what beams actually passed through
Rain, spray, fog, snow, dust, exhaust Clutter near the sensor; false obstacles; shorter range Low-intensity, low-density, short-lived clusters; per-frame return rate Persistence requirement for obstacles; density filter; weather data in training (nuScenes); degrade and raise a flag
Specular surfaces (wet road, puddles, glass) Missing returns, or mirrored points below the road Points > 0.3 m below local ground with low intensity Mark SUSPICIOUS, not depression, unless confirmed from several viewpoints
Dark or absorptive surfaces (black cars) Dropouts; object partly invisible NaN regions inside tracked boxes A NaN ray is not free space; clearing uses only real returns beyond the cell
Retroreflectors (signs, plates) Blooming; enlarged objects Saturated intensity patches Clip the intensity feature; shrink saturated clusters
Moving objects Smeared ghosts in the map Moving label or point inside a moving track Bypass the static map; τ = 0; visibility clearing

29.2 Geometry, time and coordinates

Failure Effect How to detect it Mitigation
Extrinsic calibration error 0.5° of roll gives 0.87 m height error at 100 m Ground-plane residual growing with range Start-up calibration check; online ground levelling
Timestamp offset between LiDAR and pose 10 ms at 20 m/s shifts points by 20 cm Scan-to-map residual correlated with speed PTP synchronisation; estimate the offset offline; interpolate poses
Motion distortion without deskew A 100 ms scan at 20 m/s smears by up to 2 m; 30 °/s yaw smears 2.6 m at 50 m Seam at the scan's start azimuth Per-point deskew (P7)
Pose loss or odometry failure Map smears ICP fitness; pose jumps Fail-soft: single-scan mode, reset fusion, raise a flag
Odometry drift Doubled curbs, thick poles Roughness spikes on known flat ground Drift while a cell stays inside level ℓ is bounded by about 2·E_ℓ·ε (ε = relative drift rate); decay; per-scan vertical bias alignment to the map; measure local relative error, not only the KITTI drift metric
float32 world coordinates At a UTM northing of 5 × 10⁶ m, float32 steps are 0.5 m Unit test All float32 maths relative to a float64 map anchor; re-anchor far from it
int16 elevation range ±327 m around the anchor Overflow check Re-anchor z after large altitude changes
16-bit cell timestamps Wrap every 655 s Unit test Modular differences; anything older than 600 s is stale anyway (decay ≈ 0)
◆ Array layout and conventions Column-major export; degrees vs radians; T_world_sensor vs T_sensor_world; 1-based indices Data-validation tests (§34.4) One converter, tested against golden files
◆ IDs stored as floats IDs above 2²⁴ corrupted (your road) ID round-trip test Unsigned integer fields

29.3 Resolution and representation

Failure Effect How to detect it Mitigation
Seams at level borders Height steps or class changes along straight lines Seam metric Blend band and ghost cells (§13.5)
Popping when the map recentres Cells change abruptly Pops per recentre Hysteresis; push-down inheritance flagged INPAINTED
Thin structures at coarse levels Poles vanish Thin-object recall per level Max aggregation; any-rule; objects as boxes
Objects straddling levels Inconsistent footprints Box vs map footprint IoU Objects stay in the object list; never rebuilt from cells
Mixed cells Wrong class; dilated footprints Cell purity Evidence voting; dilation bounded by s_ℓ and measured

29.4 Perception and terrain

Failure Effect How to detect it Mitigation
Class confusion (road / sidewalk, terrain / vegetation) Wrong drivable area Confusion matrix per band Evidence accumulation; geometric curb check; class-group metrics
Overconfidence Confident wrong labels Expected calibration error Temperature scaling on validation data
Rare or unknown objects Missed obstacles Recall on "other obstacle" Geometric fallback: any non-ground point > 0.15 m above ground is an obstacle
Domain shift (simulation to real, new sensor) Accuracy drop Per-domain metrics; class-histogram drift Beam dropout, intensity removal, mixed training; report domains separately
Ground hidden under cars Holes Coverage Pull–push, flagged INPAINTED; planners penalise inpainted cells
Vegetation over ground Ground estimate too high High variance plus vegetation class Use the lowest ground-candidate points in vegetation cells; flag
Ramps read as obstacles; low curbs missed Wrong traversability Slope continuity vs step A step needs a class change and a height jump above twice the level's noise
Potholes and negative obstacles Invisible, hidden by their own rim Unobserved patch inside observed road SUSPICIOUS state (§8.4)

29.5 Map accumulation and system

Failure Effect How to detect it Mitigation
Ghosts of moved objects Phantom obstacles Cells crossed by beams but not hit Visibility clearing
Stale data Outdated map Cell age layer Lazy decay
Correlated repeated observations A static point seen 100 times looks like 100 samples Weight vs number of distinct scans Weight cap; confidence from scan count, not point count
Evidence saturation, label flicker Classes never change, or change every frame Saturated weights; label change rate Cap plus decay; evidence hysteresis
Slow first frames (sparse-conv algorithm selection) Latency spikes Per-frame timings Warm-up frames; cache tuned algorithms
GPU out of memory in dense scenes Crash Memory statistics Point cap per scan; preallocated buffers
Queue build-up; visualiser back-pressure Growing latency; stalls Queue age Latest-wins input; visualiser in its own process, allowed to drop frames

30Section 30: Research contribution

30.1 What is established

Sparse convolutional segmentation (MinkowskiNet, SPVNAS/SPVCNN, Cylinder3D), centre-based detection (CenterPoint), robot-centric probabilistic elevation mapping (Fankhauser et al.; the GPU version elevation_mapping_cupy by Miki et al.), multi-level surface maps, octree and VDB maps (OctoMap, VDB-based mapping), multi-resolution occupancy maps (for example wavemap), polar and cylindrical LiDAR representations (PolarNet, Cylinder3D), ground segmentation (Patchwork++), traversability learning, and clipmaps themselves (Tanner et al. 1998; geometry clipmaps, Losasso and Hoppe 2004) are all prior work. None of them is a contribution of this project, and each area needs a proper literature search before any claim is written down.

Element Status Comment
Sparse U-Net semantics, centre-based boxes, Kalman tracking Established Reuse and cite
Clipmap as a data structure Established in graphics; used in some mapping systems Reuse and cite
Real-time integration into a semantic 2.5D pipeline Engineering Valuable, not novel by itself
Mergeable-statistics cells with exact nesting and exact temporal merge Engineering, possibly a minor contribution Depends on the literature search
Resolution law derived from sensor sampling, with a rule for n, L and s₀, validated across sensor sweeps Potentially novel Needs E5 and a clear prediction that can fail
Rate–distortion benchmark of 2.5D representations with a common query protocol Potentially novel as a benchmark Needs E1–E3 on public data and released code
Controlled distance and occlusion study linking points per object to map-level obstacle recall per level Potentially novel as an analysis Needs E4 with simulation ground truth
Risk-adaptive refinement Speculative Only with a positive result at equal budget (AO2)

30.2 Hypotheses and how they can fail

Hypothesis Test Falsified if
H1: at equal memory, the clipmap lies on or above the uniform-grid Pareto frontier for distance-weighted obstacle recall and elevation RMSE E1, E2 A 1024² uniform grid lies within the confidence interval on all metrics
H2: the best schedule follows n ≈ 2 / √(Δφ·Δθ) and moves with the sensor as predicted E5 The empirical optimum does not track the sensor's angular resolution
H3: beyond some range r*, map-level obstacle recall is limited by the sensor, not by cell size E4 with several s_ℓ Finer distant cells still raise recall
H4: temporal fusion fills the fovea, and elevation error on observed cells approaches the sensor noise floor AB7 in simulation Coverage or error plateaus far from those levels
H5: semantic ground selection lowers elevation error near obstacles compared with geometric ground AB2, AB5 No significant difference

30.3 Directions worth publishing

Planner-in-the-loop evaluation in simulation (does map fidelity change collision and comfort metrics, and at what memory?), uncertainty-aware inpainting with calibrated variances, task-aware learned level schedules, and a released benchmark of simulated scenarios with the evaluation code. A well-run negative result, such as "a 10 cm uniform grid to 50 m is enough for urban driving at 10 Hz", is also a useful benchmark finding if the protocol is strong.

31Section 31: Implementation roadmap

Eleven phases. Effort estimates assume one experienced engineer working full time and are rough; training time depends on your GPUs. Perception (P5) can run in parallel with the grid work (P2–P4), because the grid is developed and evaluated with ground-truth labels first.

P0: Foundations and data access (1–2 weeks)

Objective One loader for every data source, visible in a viewer, validated
Tasks Repository skeleton (§39); uv and Docker environments (§33); CI with lint, type checks and unit tests; readers for your ASCII PCD (column-major), the binary simulation layout, KITTI .bin/.label and nuScenes; MATLAB exporter fixes (§21.5–21.6); data-validation suite (§34.4); Rerun raw viewer (points by class, intensity or range; range image)
Depends on Nothing
Outputs io/, core/types.py, scripts/convert_pcd.py, scripts/validate_data.py, a validation report, a first simulated sequence of at least 200 frames with poses
Tests Reader round trips; golden counts for frame_00008 (§34.3); layout and pose checks
Exit gate Every source loads into RawScan (binary in < 20 ms per frame) and displays; validation passes on simulation, SemanticKITTI 08 and nuScenes mini

P1: Geometry and preprocessing (1–2 weeks)

Objective Clean, levelled, correctly framed points and a synthetic test world
Tasks Frames S / B / M / W with a float64 anchor; ego filter; levelling; crop; range image with NaN mask; NumPy ray caster with configurable beams and noise; synthetic scenes (plane, ramp, curb, pole, box, overhang, pit); timing utility; sensor/ and dataset/ config groups
Depends on P0
Outputs preprocess/, core/geometry.py, tests/synthetic/
Tests Transform round trips; ego filter removes all actor-1 points in simulation; ray caster reproduces ring spacing r²·Δθ/h within 1 %
Exit gate Preprocessing ≤ 3 ms on GPU for 227 k points; synthetic scenes available as test fixtures

P2: Grid engine and recentring (2–3 weeks)

Objective The clipmap and its baselines, correct by construction and fast
Tasks GridSpec; integer lattice and ownership masks; Clipmap on PyTorch tensors with toroidal offsets; UniformGrid and TwoLevelGrid; vectorised insertion (scatter_add_, scatter_reduce_ with amin/amax); pooling up the pyramid; recentring with hysteresis and optional look-ahead; lazy decay; nearest, bilinear and blended queries; snapshots, memory accounting, delta + zstd serialisation
Depends on P1
Outputs grid/, configs/grid/
Tests Invariants I1–I6, I8, I9 (§34.2); CPU reference vs GPU equality
Exit gate All invariants pass on 10⁴ random cases; insertion < 1 ms for 100 k points; recentring < 1 ms; your frame touches exactly 15,812 cells (6,614 / 5,474 / 2,573 / 1,151 per level)

P3: Terrain and map products (2 weeks)

Objective Every map layer a consumer needs, without seams
Tasks Gated ground mean; obstacle bottom and top; cell states; pull–push filling; slope, step, roughness, clearance, depression; traversability; blend band and ghost cells; dirty-tile derivation; Patchwork++ baseline; Rerun layer views
Depends on P2
Outputs terrain/, BEV layer views
Tests Exact reconstruction of noiseless planes and ramps; curb step error < 1 cm without noise; invariants I7, I10
Exit gate Derivation ≤ 5 ms; seam metric ≤ 1.1 on a synthetic ramp crossing all levels

P4: Evaluation harness and oracle study (2–3 weeks), ends at MVP

Objective Answer the central question, whether foveation pays off, using exact labels
Tasks Reference raster builder (§21.3) for simulation and SemanticKITTI; query protocol; metric library; distance bands; Parquet schema; polar and 3D-voxel baselines; experiment E1 with B0–B7, G1 and G2; Pareto plots with confidence intervals; first sensor sweep and distance ladder in simulation
Depends on P3
Outputs eval/, results/e1/, an architecture decision record with the go / no-go
Tests Metrics on hand-computed toy cases; reference builder checked against the simulation road mesh
Exit gate Milestone M1 (§32). If the clipmap does not pay off, switch to the winning baseline: the rest of the plan still applies because every grid shares one interface

P5: Perception v1 (3–4 weeks, parallel with P2–P4)

Objective A competitive per-point semantic network in the project taxonomy
Tasks Datasets and augmentation (§22.2); sparse U-Net with point branch; train first on the standard 19 SemanticKITTI classes and compare with a reference code base; then switch to the 10-class taxonomy; inference wrapper; prediction cache; temperature calibration; distance-binned metrics; simulation fine-tuning with and without intensity
Depends on P1
Outputs models/, perception/, datasets/, first registered checkpoint
Tests Overfitting a single batch; shapes and dtypes; yaw-rotation consistency; determinism in test mode; label-map coverage
Exit gate 19-class validation mIoU within about 3 points of the reference code's reported value for a comparable model; 10-class model ≤ 40 ms FP16 on 120 k points

P6: Integrated single-scan pipeline (1–2 weeks), ends at Prototype

Objective Raw scan in, labelled foveated map out, visible live
Tasks Stage composition; synchronous runner; health flags and fail-soft fallbacks; NVTX ranges and per-frame timing log; full Rerun dashboard (§25); experiment E2 in single-scan mode
Depends on P4, P5
Outputs pipeline/, viz/, scripts/replay.py
Tests 50-frame integration replays on simulation and SemanticKITTI
Exit gate Milestone M2: runs on your exports, simulation and SemanticKITTI; end-to-end ≤ 150 ms before optimisation

P7: Temporal processing (2–3 weeks)

Objective A fused map that fills the fovea and forgets what has moved
Tasks Pose adapters (simulation ground truth, dataset poses, KISS-ICP); deskew; decayed accumulation; visibility clearing; moving points bypass the static map; asynchronous runner with latest-wins queue; drift and timestamp-offset checks
Depends on P6
Outputs temporal/ (fusion, clearing, odometry)
Tests A static scene converges to ground truth; a car that drives away leaves no ghost after k frames; decay composition (I6); asynchronous and synchronous runners agree in deterministic mode
Exit gate Level-0 coverage curve vs distance driven reported; ghost rate below the threshold set in the analysis plan; no latency growth over a 30-minute replay

P8: Objects and tracking (3–4 weeks)

Objective Resolution-independent objects with identities and motion
Tasks BEV clustering first; centre-based head trained on nuScenes (stage C); box decoding; Kalman tracker; motion state; objects in snapshots; experiment E4 in simulation
Depends on P7
Outputs Tracker module, detection head checkpoint, recall-vs-distance results
Tests Tracker on synthetic trajectories (no ID switches without occlusion); head overfitting; peak extraction and NMS tests
Exit gate AP and AMOTA per distance band; moving objects absent from static layers

P9: Multi-task learning and optimisation (3–4 weeks), ends at Advanced prototype

Objective The full model at 10 Hz
Tasks Ground-height head (stage B) fused with pull–push; joint training (stage D) and simulation mixing (stage E); profiling (§35); kernel fixes; FP16; TensorRT / libspconv export and parity test
Depends on P8, and P3 for the pull–push comparison
Outputs Optimised pipeline, TensorRT engines, profiling reports
Tests Parity (§36.2); performance tests against the budget
Exit gate Milestone M3: mean ≤ 60 ms and p99 ≤ 100 ms on the workstation; the ground head improves error on inpainted cells or is removed

The ground-height head comes after objects in this plan, although it is stage B in §22.4, because it only earns its latency once there is a pull–push baseline to beat.

P10: Final research system (4–6 weeks)

Objective Results, deployment and documentation you can hand over
Tasks Experiments E1–E5 on all datasets; essential ablations, optional ones as time allows; C++/CUDA runtime; Jetson deployment; ROS 2 adapter and live Simulink demo; documentation (§38); reproducibility package (§37); final report
Depends on P9
Outputs cpp/, ros2/, deployment images, results/, report
Exit gate Milestone M4: every table and figure regenerated by one command; Jetson latency and power measured

Total: roughly 24–35 weeks.

32Section 32: Milestones

Milestone After Includes Deliberately excludes Demonstrates Accepted when
M1 MVP P4 (≈ 8–12 weeks) Readers, preprocessing, clipmap and baselines, terrain products, evaluation harness, oracle labels Neural networks, temporal fusion, objects, optimisation Whether foveation pays off, measured on exact data Invariants pass; Pareto plots with confidence intervals; seam metric ≤ 1.1; go / no-go recorded
M2 Prototype P6 + learned semantics, single-scan pipeline, dashboard Temporal fusion, tracking, TensorRT The whole chain from raw points to a labelled foveated map Runs on three data sources; semantic metrics per band; ≤ 150 ms per frame
M3 Advanced prototype P9 + fusion, clearing, objects, tracking, ground head, optimisation Edge hardware, ROS 2 A real-time system with fused map and objects Workstation latency targets; coverage and ghost-rate targets; AP per band
M4 Final research system P10 + edge deployment, ROS 2 and Simulink, full evaluation and ablations, documentation Safety certification, production hardening Research results and a reusable system Reproducible tables; Jetson measurements; complete documentation

The MVP contains no deep learning on purpose. The central claim of the project is about the representation, and ground-truth labels test that claim cheaply and without perception noise. If the claim fails, about two months are spent and every component except the level schedule remains useful.

33Section 33: Environment setup

Version numbers below are lower bounds or examples; the lock file records the exact set that passed the smoke test. Wheel names for PyTorch and spconv depend on your CUDA version, so check them on the projects' install pages before running the commands.

33.1 Host (Ubuntu 22.04)

# NVIDIA driver; afterwards nvidia-smi must report a CUDA version ≥ the wheels' CUDA version

sudo ubuntu-drivers install

33.5 Jetson AGX Orin

Flash JetPack 6.x (Ubuntu 22.04-based, with CUDA 12 and TensorRT). On the device, the deployed network runs as TensorRT engines with sparse layers through NVIDIA's libspconv, and the grid engine is the C++/CUDA runtime built natively from the same CMake project. Install PyTorch only for debugging, from NVIDIA's Jetson builds or the jetson-containers images. Set the maximum power mode with sudo nvpmodel -m 0 && sudo jetson_clocks for benchmarks, and log tegrastats during every run.

33.6 MATLAB side

MATLAB R2023b or newer with Automated Driving Toolbox; RoadRunner for terrain scenes; ROS Toolbox for live streaming (optional). Keep the exporter in the repository's matlab/ folder next to the Python reader, and write the exporter version into meta.yaml, so the two cannot drift apart.

34Section 34: Testing strategy

34.1 Test layers

Layer Scope Tooling When
Unit Transforms, quantisation, readers, metrics pytest Every commit (CPU)
Property Grid invariants (§34.2) Hypothesis Every commit; a long profile nightly
Synthetic scenes Ray-cast scenes with analytic ground truth pytest fixtures Every commit
Golden files Counts from your frame; outputs on a small simulated sequence pytest Every commit
Integration 50-frame replays through the whole pipeline (simulation, SemanticKITTI 08 subset) pytest on a GPU runner Nightly
Performance Stage timings vs budget; memory pytest-benchmark, NVTX Nightly; fail if p95 regresses by > 10 %
Accuracy regression Mini-benchmark metrics within tolerance bands Stored Parquet baselines Nightly and before merging model or grid changes
Model Single-batch overfitting, shapes, rotation consistency, export parity, calibration pytest On model changes
Data validation Schemas, ranges, layout, poses (§34.4) scripts/validate_data.py On every new dataset or export
C++/CUDA (later) Kernel results equal the PyTorch reference GoogleTest + pytest Every commit on the GPU runner

34.2 Grid invariants

ID Invariant
I1 Nesting idx_{ℓ+1}(x) = ⌊idx_ℓ(x) / 2⌋ for every x inside the extents
I2 Partition Every x inside E_{L−1} is owned by exactly one level
I3 Merge exactness Pooling level ℓ by 2 × 2 equals inserting directly into level ℓ+1: exact for counts, minima and maxima; relative 10⁻⁶ for float sums
I4 Order independence Inserting A ∪ B equals inserting A then B, for any split into chunks
I5 Scroll invariance A query at world point x is identical before and after recentring, for x inside both windows
I6 Decay composition decay(Δt₁) followed by decay(Δt₂) equals decay(Δt₁ + Δt₂)
I7 Plane reproduction A noiseless plane (slope < 30°) is reconstructed within 1 mm on observed cells at every level, and the blended query is continuous across borders
I8 Memory memory_bytes() equals the formula in §14.3
I9 Device equality GPU results equal the CPU reference
I10 Empty is not free A cell no beam has reached stays UNKNOWN 
import torch
from hypothesis import given, settings, strategies as st
from foveamap.grid import Clipmap, ClipmapSpec

SPEC = ClipmapSpec(n=64, levels=4, s0=0.05)          # small n keeps tests fast
coord = st.floats(-SPEC.extent(3) + 1e-3, SPEC.extent(3) - 1e-3, allow_nan=False)

@given(x=coord, y=coord)
def test_nesting(x, y):                                # I1
    p = torch.tensor([[x, y]], dtype=torch.float64)
    for level in range(SPEC.levels - 1):
        child = SPEC.lattice_index(p, level)
        parent = SPEC.lattice_index(p, level + 1)
        assert torch.equal(torch.div(child, 2, rounding_mode="floor"), parent)

@settings(max_examples=200, deadline=None)
@given(n=st.integers(1, 5000), seed=st.integers(0, 2**31 - 1))
def test_merge_exact(n, seed):                         # I3
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    pts = (torch.rand(n, 3, generator=g) - 0.5) * 2 * SPEC.extent(0)
    fine, coarse = Clipmap(SPEC), Clipmap(SPEC)
    fine.insert_level(pts, level=0)
    coarse.insert_level(pts, level=1)
    pooled = fine.pool(level=0)                        # 2×2 merge, level-1 cell layout
    ref = coarse.level(1).center_crop(SPEC.n // 2)     # the part level 0 covers
    assert torch.equal(pooled.count, ref.count)
    assert torch.equal(pooled.zmax, ref.zmax)
    torch.testing.assert_close(pooled.sum_z, ref.sum_z, rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-6)

The implementation quantises each point once onto the s₀ lattice and derives coarser indices by integer shifts, so I1 holds by construction. Keep the test anyway: it guards against later changes such as per-level anchors or cell sizes read from separate config values.

34.3 Synthetic scenes and golden files

A small NumPy ray caster with configurable beam tables and noise renders analytic scenes (plane, ramp, curb, pole, box, overhang, pit) whose ground truth is known exactly; these are the fixtures for terrain and seam tests. Your frame becomes a golden file with these expected values: 227,351 points; 52,878 valid; 30,062 ego; 4,383 car, 2,785 truck, 4 bicycle, 299 pedestrian, 635 barrier and 14,710 road points; 84,279 scatter writes; 15,812 touched cells (6,614 / 5,474 / 2,573 / 1,151 per level).

34.4 Data validation

Check Catches
dtype and shape per field Wrong exporter settings
NaN ratio per frame inside the expected band Sensor or export faults
Azimuth increases along the columns of the organised scan Column-major vs row-major mix-ups (your current files)
Elevation decreases down the rows Flipped rows
Labels inside the taxonomy; IDs are integers < 2¹⁶ Float IDs, unmapped classes
RᵀR ≈ I (10⁻⁵), det R = +1, translation steps consistent with speed Wrong pose convention, jumps
Timestamps increasing, spacing ≈ 100 ms Dropped frames
Ground-plane height matches the sensor mount Wrong frame
Ego-actor points only inside the ego box Missing or wrong ego ID
A classifier on intensity alone scores below 90 % Label leakage through synthetic intensity

35Section 35: Profiling and optimisation

35.1 Tools

Layer Tool Use
Python CPU py-spy (py-spy record --native -o prof.svg -- python scripts/replay.py), cProfile Flame graphs; attach to a running pipeline with py-spy dump --pid
GPU operators PyTorch Profiler (record_shapes, profile_memory, Chrome trace export) Dominant operators; hidden host–device synchronisations
System timeline Nsight Systems (nsys profile -t cuda,nvtx,osrt -o run python scripts/replay.py) CPU/GPU interplay, copies, idle gaps, stage ranges
Kernels Nsight Compute Custom CUDA kernels only
Host memory memray Allocation peaks, leaks in long replays
GPU memory torch.cuda.memory_stats, memory snapshots (torch.cuda.memory._record_memory_history) Peaks and fragmentation
I/O py-spy, iostat, strace -c Reader stalls
C++ runtime perf; Tracy (optional) Deployment code
Jetson tegrastats, jtop Power, thermal throttling, memory
End to end Per-frame Parquet log from sensor timestamp to publication Latency percentiles, drops

35.2 Measuring correctly

CUDA runs asynchronously, so wall-clock timing without synchronisation charges work to the wrong stage. Record CUDA events per stage and resolve them with one synchronisation per frame; never call .item() or .cpu() inside a stage unless the design requires it. Discard at least 50 warm-up frames (sparse-convolution algorithm selection, allocator growth), and report p50 / p95 / p99 rather than the mean alone.

import torch
import torch.cuda.nvtx as nvtx
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def stage(name: str, events: list):
    start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
    end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
    nvtx.range_push(name)
    start.record()
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        end.record()
        nvtx.range_pop()
        events.append((name, start, end))

def resolve(events: list) -> dict[str, float]:          # once per frame
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    return {name: s.elapsed_time(e) for name, s, e in events}   # milliseconds

35.3 Procedure

  1. Fix the budget (§18.2) and the replay sets (500 simulated frames; the first 1,000 frames of SemanticKITTI 08).
  2. Record a Nsight Systems timeline and the per-stage log.
  3. Rank stages by how far their p95 exceeds the budget; work on the worst one only.
  4. Fix in this order: do less work (algorithm) → move less data (copies, synchronisations) → remove Python loops → better or fused kernels → lower precision.
  5. Measure again. Keep a change only if p95 improves and the accuracy regression suite still passes.
  6. Stop once the budget is met.

35.4 Candidate optimisations

Stage Candidates Expected effect (to verify)
Ingest Binary format, memory-mapped files, pinned buffers Removes seconds-per-frame ASCII parsing
Preprocessing Fused GPU operations, torch.compile Small
Voxelisation GPU hashing instead of sort-based unique 1–2 ms
Network FP16, algorithm tuning, channel width, fewer full-resolution layers, TensorRT / libspconv The largest gain
Post-processing Peak extraction by max-pooling, no Python loops Milliseconds
Grid In-place scatters, preallocated buffers, dirty-tile derivation, custom kernels Milliseconds
Temporal Clearing on a second CUDA stream Parallelism
Publishing Delta encoding, zstd level 1–3, background thread Milliseconds and bandwidth
Visualisation Decimation, separate process Removes stalls

CUDA graphs help little for the sparse backbone because its shapes change every frame; the dense heads can use them.

36Section 36: Deployment

36.1 Targets

Target Hardware Runtime Configuration Goal
Development workstation RTX 4080 class, 16 GB PyTorch FP16, Python pipeline Full model; L = 4, n = 512 Fast iteration, replays, dashboard
High-performance real time RTX 4090 / RTX 6000 Ada class TensorRT engines + C++ grid engine, or PyTorch FP16 if it meets the budget Full model; room for a wider backbone or several sensors 10 Hz with headroom
Edge Jetson AGX Orin 32 / 64 GB TensorRT FP16/INT8, libspconv, C++/CUDA grid engine, ROS 2 Width × 0.5 or range-image backbone; 10 cm voxels; L = 3 or n = 384; detection at 5 Hz p99 ≤ 100 ms with measured power

36.2 Model conversion

PyTorch checkpoint (FP32)
 ├─ dense parts (BEV heads, point MLPs) ─► ONNX ─► TensorRT engine (FP16 / INT8)
 └─ sparse backbone ─► a) NVIDIA libspconv / spconv C++ runtime (weights exported layer by layer)
                       b) fallback: LibTorch FP16 inside the C++ host (simplest, slower)
 ─► parity gate: per-point argmax agreement ≥ 99.5 % vs FP32,
                 box AP drop ≤ 0.5 points, ground-height error increase ≤ 5 mm

For INT8, calibrate after training on 500–1,000 frames stratified by dataset, distance and scene type; keep the first layer, the last layer and the heads in FP16 if parity fails; use quantisation-aware training only if the loss still exceeds 1 mIoU. TensorRT engines are tied to the GPU model and TensorRT version, so build them on the target device.

The grid engine moves from the PyTorch reference to C++17/CUDA kernels (insert, pool, decay, clear, derive) with nanobind bindings, so the Python pipeline can call the same kernels; equality tests against the reference (I9) guard the port.

36.3 Runtime layout and interfaces

On the workstation, the pipeline is one Python process plus a visualiser process. On the edge device, one C++ process runs reader, inference, grid engine and tracker, and publishes over ROS 2; visualisation runs off-board through the Foxglove bridge.

Direction Interface
Input points sensor_msgs/PointCloud2, organised, with ring and per-point time fields
Input pose tf2 (odom → base_link)
Output map grid_map_msgs/GridMap per level (the grid_map library supports ROS 2), or a compact custom message carrying all levels as deltas
Output objects vision_msgs/Detection3DArray with track IDs
Health diagnostic_msgs plus a latency topic

Simulink publishes the same point-cloud and pose messages through ROS Toolbox, so the live demo needs no special code path.

36.4 Packaging and operation

Build three images: dev (x86, CUDA devel, tools), runtime-x86 (slim, engines built on the target) and runtime-l4t (on an L4T base). Per-target settings live in configs/deploy/. Monitor latency, drops, GPU temperature, map coverage and whether a fallback is active. This is a research prototype: it is not safety-certified and must not control a vehicle on public roads without a separately validated safety layer.

foveamap/
├── pyproject.toml  requirements.lock  Makefile  README.md  LICENSE
├── configs/                    Hydra config groups
│   ├── sensor/                 beam tables and extrinsics (matlab_101x2251.yaml, hdl64.yaml, …)

│   ├── io/                     PCD (incl. column-major), KITTI, simulation layout, nuScenes, MCAP

│   ├── preprocess/             ego filter, crop, deskew, levelling, range image
│   ├── models/                 voxeliser, backbone, point branch, heads, losses, multi-task wrapper
│   ├── perception/             inference wrapper, prediction cache, clustering, box decoding, calibration
│   ├── grid/                   GridSpec, Clipmap, UniformGrid, TwoLevelGrid, PolarGrid, accumulators, queries, serialisation
│   ├── terrain/                ground, pull–push, features, traversability, Patchwork++ baseline
│   ├── temporal/               pose adapters, KISS-ICP wrapper, fusion and decay, visibility clearing, tracker
│   ├── pipeline/               stages, sync and async runners, health, fallbacks
│   ├── viz/                    Rerun logging, colour maps, comparison views

│   └── ros2/                   adapter nodes (P10)
├── cpp/                        C++17/CUDA runtime: grid kernels, TensorRT/libspconv inference, nanobind bindings, GoogleTest
├── matlab/                     exporter, scenario generators, RoadRunner notes, Simulink streaming model
├── scripts/                    convert_pcd, validate_data, build_manifest, train, infer, replay, bench,
│                               run_experiment, make_report, export_trt
├── tests/
│   ├── unit/  property/  synthetic/  golden/  integration/
│   └── performance/  model/  data/
├── docs/                       MkDocs site, ADRs, dataset and model cards, guides
├── docker/                     dev, runtime-x86, runtime-l4t
├── data/                       git-ignored raw data; manifests tracked by DVC
├── cache/                      git-ignored prediction caches and reference rasters
├── models/                     registry.yaml (checkpoints stored outside git)
├── results/                    Parquet results and generated figures
└── .github/workflows/          CI: CPU checks on every push, GPU suite nightly on a self-hosted runner

The package directories match the modules in §24.1 one to one. Three choices in this layout are deliberate. cache/ exists so that every grid experiment can run without loading the network, which keeps representation studies fast and free of model randomness. matlab/ lives in the same repository as the Python reader so the file format cannot silently drift between the two. cpp/ has its own CMake build and only enters the picture in P10, so the research code never waits for compilation.

41Section 41: Final recommended architecture

Component Choice
Input Any spinning LiDAR, organised if possible, plus a pose source; your MATLAB exports in the SemanticKITTI-style layout
Preprocessing Validity mask kept, ego filter, deskew, levelling, float64 map anchor
Perception Sparse 3D U-Net (spconv, 10 cm voxels) with a point branch; heads for 10-class semantics, 40 cm ground height with uncertainty, centre-based boxes, optional motion
Objects Boxes with a Kalman tracker; moving points kept out of the static map
Map Clipmap with 4 levels, n = 512, cells of 5 / 10 / 20 / 40 cm covering ±12.8 / ±25.6 / ±51.2 / ±102.4 m; one integer lattice; toroidal scrolling; recentring with hysteresis
Cell Accumulators (weights, Σz, Σz², min / max, class evidence, time) and derived products (ground, obstacle bottom and top, class, confidence, traversability, flags); 12 bytes core, 48 bytes extended
Terrain Semantic ground selection, geometric features, pull–push filling, plus the network prior if it earns its place
Temporal Lazy decay, visibility clearing, weight caps
Real time 10 Hz; one GPU loop with a latest-wins queue; visualiser in its own process
Software Python 3.10, PyTorch, Hydra, Rerun, pytest with Hypothesis, uv, Docker; C++/CUDA and TensorRT for deployment; ROS 2 adapter
Data MATLAB simulation for exact ground truth and controlled studies; SemanticKITTI as the main benchmark; nuScenes for objects
Evaluation Common query protocol, distance bands, rate–distortion curves against equal-budget uniform grids

This combination is recommended because each part answers a measured fact rather than a preference. Your sensor's sample spacing grows linearly with range, and the clipmap follows that law with dense arrays, exact nesting and constant-time lookup. A single scan fills only 4 % of the 5 cm cells within 10 m, so the design depends on fusion, filling and an explicit unknown state instead of pretending the fovea is dense. Distant objects get a handful of points, so they are detected on the points and stored as boxes instead of waiting for finer cells. The sparse voxel network is the proven accuracy-per-millisecond choice for outdoor LiDAR, and keeping it separate from the grid lets the representation be judged with exact labels.

Three questions remain open by design and are settled by experiments rather than argument: whether the clipmap beats an equal-budget uniform grid for your use case (E1, milestone M1), which level schedule suits your target sensor (AB1, E5), and whether risk-based refinement adds anything beyond distance (AO2).

The first concrete work is steps 1–3: set up the environment, turn your current frame into a golden test, and fix the MATLAB exporter so the next sequence you generate arrives in the format the rest of the system expects.

Sections 0–41. Numbers marked as budgets or targets are to be measured; numbers about frame_00008.pcd were measured on your file.
